en: | | Praise in a Garland of Metres ||
Accompanied by an exposition of the *Vṛttamālā*.
Oṃ. Homage to Mañjuśrī.
We pay homage to Jñānaśrīmitra, who is born from the splendor of knowledge,
like a garland of verses from a treasury of intellects.

Here, this Jñānaśrīmitra— who has reached the furthest limit of the multitude of his virtues and knowledge— desiring to offer praise to the noble Mañjuśrī, who is the very essence of existence, and wishing to explain the various types of meters according to his own will by means of the designations of ascetic bodies,
first provides a general introduction to the classification of the meters to be explained,
beginning with the words "vṛttam" and so forth.

The masters of speech declare that *vṛtta* is of three kinds—equal, half-equal, and unequal—and for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others, it is, in brief, threefold, while in detail, it is infinite. (1)
The lords of speech, Mañjuśrī, recite, consider, or teach your life story and conduct;
the "lords of sages" (munīndra) are to be understood as the subject.
To the question of what that [life story] is like, he says:
"Equal" (sama) means having a peaceful form;
"half-equal" (ardhasama) means having a slightly wrathful form; "unequal" (viṣama) means having a fierce wrathful form.
Thus, they describe your conduct in this way as being of three kinds in brief;
however, in detail, it is infinite because each one is infinite.
To the question "For what purpose? he says:
For the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others; that is, for the purpose of performing what is beneficial for others.
In the case of *vṛtta*, however, Vāgīśa [is the authority],
as are the sages Piṅgala and others;
*vṛtta* refers to a specific type of verse (*padya*).
The *sama* [meters] begin with *vaiśvadevī*;
the *ardhasama* [meters] begin with *upacitrā*;
and the *viṣama* [meters] begin with *padacaturūrdhva*.
Thus, they traditionally teach that [the path] is threefold in brief.
Even here, because each of the *samādīs* is infinite, it is infinite.
As it has been said: "This path of verses is infinite; this distinction is for the sake of the beauty of the recitation."
"Methods for the sake of others" (*parārthavidhi*) is as explained previously.
Alternatively, "the other" (*para*) refers to the "excellent" (*prakṛṣṭa*) object;
it is for the sake of the method for that, that is, for the purpose of its exposition.
For when a subject matter is composed in metrical form, it becomes easy to understand.
Furthermore, he states what that conduct (*vṛtta*) is like,
beginning with the words "pratiniyata" and so forth.
In this [work], the recitation of names, which has arisen with distinct forms, shines forth as the supreme meter and verse through various arrangements. (2)

In which [contexts], within those specific behaviors, forms, and physical manifestations, the names that have become established and well-known are chanted together and proclaimed by the eminent sages, the Buddhas; there, designations such as "Stiracakrā" and others are composed, and therein lies the metrical structure (chandas),
which is to say, the intended expression.
"It manifests for those who behold it"— this is the ellipsis.
"The supreme state" means that the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*) and the established order (*vyavasthiti*) manifest as the most excellent.
How does it manifest?
It manifests through not overstepping those various arrangements that are superimpositions according to the inclinations of sentient beings;
the sense is that this is because [the teaching] is partial to these eight aspects.
In the case of *vṛtta* (metrical verse), however, the name is well-known— that is, established— among specific forms characterized by a fixed sequence of heavy and light syllables.
This has been celebrated by the eminent sages such as Piṅgala and others, as in [the verses beginning] "This Vaiśvī, this Tanumadhyā," and so forth.

And where there is *chandas* (metrical form) designated as *gāyatrī* and so forth—how is it that those various arrangements (*vinyāsa*) receive the designations of *gāyatrī* and so on? It is by not deviating from them;
and "of the feet" refers to the pause (*yati*).
And that [rhythm] shines forth in its excellence;
here too, it should be understood as "according to various arrangements.
This is because of the statement: "A pause (*viśrāma*) occurs at the half-verse, a break (*bhaṅga*) at the word, and the caesura (*yati*) at the quarter-verse, as will be explained."
Alternatively, because [the meters] such as Śuddhavirāḍārṣabha exist in positions beginning with one [syllable],
the connection with the preceding [verse] is: "The ancients declare that meter to be [defined] by those various arrangements (vinyāsa) of the *yati* according to their respective kinds."
In this context, "having specific forms" is a general introduction to the body;
"the Litany of Names" refers to the designation;
and "the word" refers to the practitioner.
And because of the word *chandas*, it means "of the Veda" (*chāndasa*).
Now, one might object: since Hari, Hara, and others possess an abundance of qualities, does not the Blessed One deserve to be praised by excluding them?
Thus, in response to the question of how that weightiness of his qualities was understood, he says "pratirūpa" and so forth.
Even by observing the outward appearance, the wise are able to calculate, in their entirety and in due order, the heavy and light [faults]; what more need be said here regarding further inquiry? (3)
"Pratirūpāḥ" means images or representations.

Even from seeing them, it is not possible for the wise to calculate or enumerate in every way—through the entire sequence—that "these teachers are heavy solely because of their form," while "these [others] are light because of the lightness of their qualities. This is due to the weightiness of their virtues and the lightness of their qualities respectively.
As it has been said: "O Lord, how wonderful is this form of yours, which brings such delight even upon a painting!
Therefore, what further purpose is there in this introduction to praise? What is gained by raising questions or by cross-examination?
The meaning is that there is nothing else.

Regarding the section on meters (*vṛttapakṣa*), one might ask: "How can there be a determination of the fixed sequence of heavy and light syllables without the technical designations such as *bha* and so forth composed by the ancient masters?
To this he says: "The forms are the sūtras and verses;
their counterparts are the *prastāras*."
This is because [the determination] is also seen from that [other method].
It is not solely by means of the technical names beginning with *bh*.
Therefore, what is the purpose of the question: "How can the determination of the sequence of heavy and light syllables be made without the technical names beginning with *bh*?"
The meaning is that [the author uses] such designations because of the prolixity of the text and the difficulty of comprehension.
Now, in order to demonstrate the purpose of the undertaking of this treatise by way of its stylistic approach, he says:
"May [the Lord] prevail," and so forth.
May this, which is being contemplated with reverence, serve to destroy the delusions of you who are born from the lineage of the virtuous—acting as the singular ornament for your own speech. 4.
Introduction.
This is the life-story of the Blessed One.
When reflected upon with reverence and practiced by you, may it serve to destroy delusion—that is, to bring about the abandonment of error.

For, having first grasped it through wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), when it is practiced through wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), the life-story of the Blessed One leads, through the excellence of that practice, to the collapse of delusion.
He asks what kind of conduct that was and says:
"By the words of those whose birthplace is the mouth of the virtuous. That is to say, their own—meaning innate, not adventitious, and unique—words.
An ornament (*ābharaṇa*) is a decoration (*alaṃkāra*) because it exists as something distinct from others;
for by the virtuous conduct of the Lord of Speech being described, the words of the righteous are indeed adorned.
Therefore, this reflection upon the conduct of the Blessed One has the purpose of dispelling misconceptions.

And since the description of that [virtue] is sufficient to adorn speech, O virtuous ones, it is fitting for you to engage in both the contemplation and the description of it; thus, the purpose for engaging in this—characterized by both visible and invisible results—has been made manifest.

As for the section on *vṛtta* (moral conduct), may this work, which contemplates moral conduct such as truthfulness and so forth with its underlying intent, serve to destroy the delusions of you, the listeners, and to eliminate ignorance regarding the subject of *vṛtta*.
Describing what that [work] is like, he says:
"By the well-composed," and so forth.
For poetic meter (*vṛtta*) is indeed an ornament of the words of poets,
since it was first introduced by Vālmīki through its being composed in metrical feet.
The purpose is to be understood as before.
Regarding the term *prastāvanā*: it means an introduction to the subject matter that is about to be expounded.
"Intellect, speech, and fortune."
Dhī is speech;
Śrī is the name. || 5 ||
The ground of one's own nature shines forth.

This meter named *Śrī* belongs to the one-syllable class of meters (*ekākṣara-chandas*). Although in the path of poetic practice usage is seen only for those beginning with six syllables and not for those beginning with one syllable due to their lack of aesthetic beauty, it has been stated in the *Padyaviveka*: "The *Ukta*, *Atyuktaka*, *Madhyā*, *Pratiṣṭhā*, and *Supratiṣṭhā* [are the names of the one-syllable meters]."
Generally, they are not relied upon because they lie outside of practical application and because of their lack of spiritual capacity.
And so Jayadeva says: "The Gāyatrī is the first of the meters. And in the Ratnākara: "They know the meters to begin with six syllables and increase by one syllable for each subsequent foot.
Here too, he will say: "The meter is like the Gāyatrī, beginning with the Sāvitrī."
Even in the *Padyālaṃkāra*, only the *gāyatrī* and other such [Vedic] meters are shown;
however, here, no name for a poetic meter (*chandaḥ-vṛtta*) has been mentioned other than through the composition of verses (*śloka-bandha*).
Nevertheless, there is no fault, as it has been indicated by way of mere possibility.
Moreover, usage is also observed elsewhere, such as:
*dhīḥ*, *śrīḥ*, *teṣām*.
Devotion to the Buddha should be practiced by all.
The Buddhist position has been refuted by means of logical arguments.
May all sentient beings, beginning with those at the head, be endowed with virtue and possessed of happiness.
Who would not honor him who carries out the command of the All-Knowing One? Indeed, what virtuous goals do they not pursue through him?
And in the *Raṅgaracanā*, it is said: "For the sake of memory, Puruṣottama has extracted a portion from Bharata and others."
In this context, *dhī* is untainted wisdom (*anāsravā prajñā*);
*gī* is blameless speech;
and *śrī* is mundane and supramundane prosperity (*sampatti*).
Among these, "own" means established by its very nature;
"one" means unique, without a second; "ground" (bhū) means the earth, the support, or the place of origin.
Its connection with what follows is that "the form of Mañjuśrī, who holds the blue lotus in his hand, is victorious."
The meter named *Sukha*, belonging to the *Vidyākṣara* class of meters which has the name *Atyuktā*, shines forth with its own unique ground.
Furthermore, he describes what that form is like:
"And it is served incessantly by those who praise its virtues."
And it is constantly attended by those who praise its virtues.

This is the *mṛgī* meter, consisting of three syllables with the middle one designated as heavy (*madhyābhidhāna*). It is not only the sole native ground for wisdom (*dhī*), speech (*gī*), and fortune (*śrī*);
it belongs to those whose nature is to desire—that is, to wish to praise—the qualities of her body, such as the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and the secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*).

It should be understood that this body is served and worshipped by those who proclaim the glorious qualities [of the Buddha] through their intellect and speech, or by the gods, asuras, and others who have gone there, as well as by the foremost among gods and men.
He asks, "Of what nature are they? and says:
"By those whose impurities have slipped from their common substratum.
That is, by those whose impurities have slipped from their common substratum (*samāśraya*).
By those arisen among the gods and asuras, etc. || 8 ||
"Having the Blessed One as their refuge" means taking refuge in the Blessed One.
For that reason, it refers to those whose stains—the afflictions such as passion and the like—have faltered.
This is the meaning.

Precisely because those foremost among the gods, asuras, and others praise the qualities of the Blessed One’s body, for that very reason she is incessantly served by them; and through their power, by means of the gradual removal of stains caused by lapses in their reliance [upon her], they come to attain those very qualities.

This is the *vṛtta* named *Jayā*, consisting of four syllables, which establishes the name *Pratiṣṭhā* through the stains of lapses arising from their common reliance among the gods, asuras, and others.
Furthermore, he asks "of what nature [are they]?
and says: "not belonging to a single existence," and so forth.
By those who properly maintain the specific excellence of awakening, which has been increased through practice throughout many lifetimes. || 9 ||
This is the *pañkti* meter named *supratiṣṭhā*, belonging to the five-syllable class (*pañcākṣara*).
Other specific varieties of the five-syllable meters, beginning with *ukta* and ending with *pratiṣṭhā*, have also been shown by Rāja;
they are to be understood from that very source.
The word *naikabhava* does not undergo elision of the *n* because it is formed with the suffix *cha*,
which is applied after the class beginning with *vṛddhi* (i.e., *taddhita* suffixes) to mean "existing therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*). Thus, the repetition [of the syllable] is *naikabhavīya*.
That specific excellence of awakening (*bodhaviśeṣa*) which has been nourished and brought to growth by him is free from defects such as error (*viparyāsa*).

By those who properly—that is, beautifully—maintain that [awakening], there is the attainment of the specific qualities of the Lord’s body, produced from merit and knowledge accumulated over many eons; for, despite the fact that [the body] possesses the impurity of faltering upon the Lord as its refuge, there is an absence of that specific excellence of intellect increased through practice over a succession of many births due to the lack of His instruction.
Thus he makes it manifest.
Furthermore, he describes what that body is like with the words beginning "song" (gīta), etc.
The Gītā is like the Gāyatrī among meters, to be savored by the virtuous; it contains the conduct that leads to future welfare and indeed possesses universal truth. 10.
That which is sung by the virtuous:
just as the *gāyatrī* meter is to be savored (*svādyā*) in its very midst from the beginning, so too is this [state] to be savored through the desire for the meter.
For the word *chandas* also denotes the function of desire.
For just as the activity of words proceeds according to one's will (*chandas*), so too in whichever body this universal excellence (*vaiśva-śreyaḥ*) has occurred— that is,
come into being.
"Bhāvi" means that which is to come into being; "sat" or "vidyamānaṃ" means that which already exists.
In the section on meters (*vṛttapakṣa*), this first [section] concerns the *gāyatrī* meter, in which this entire metrical system is contained.
It should be understood that the term "in which the *gāyatrī* meter is the primary one" applies as far as the section on refuge (*śaraṇa*) is concerned.
The phrase beginning with "nīlotpalapāṇeḥ" has been applied [as follows]: "Victorious is this slender-waisted form of the Teacher, who holds a blue lotus in his hand and whose abode is grace. (11)
Her slender waist is her abode for play and her dwelling for dalliance;
she whose waist is thus slender is "tanumadhyā" (slender-waisted).
In the square section is the Gāyatrī metre; she who is here named Tanumadhyā is its presiding deity.
"Be gracious," and so forth.
Be gracious, O Blessed One; look with favor for a moment upon this dull-witted person who has you alone as his refuge. 12.
O Blessed One, be gracious; be pleased toward one such as I. Behold this person who is dull-witted and ignorant.
Of what nature is he?
He has you alone as his refuge.
This is a qualifying attribute used as a reason, meaning "he for whom you alone are the refuge or support."
In the case of the *vṛtta* (metrical) variety, the meter is *gāyatrī*, and its name, *svādyā*, is the specific *vṛtta*.
"It blazes intensely," and so forth.
The teaching of the Sugata, having encountered you, blazes intensely;
for the unbearable radiance of the sun indeed becomes even more intense when it falls upon heat. 13.
"Having come together with you, having attained you"—
the teaching or scripture of the Sugata is *saugata*, or its meaning;
it "blazes forth," that is, it shines exceedingly.
The meaning is that it blazed forth.
The word *hi* indicates similarity;
as in the case of *uṣṇi*, which means at the time of heat.
The root *uṣ* means "to burn.
[The word *uṣas*] is derived from the *uṇādi* suffix *kanin*, because it belongs to the *puṃs* group.
[Thus, it means] the abode of the sun.

*Atireka* means excess; that which exists together with it is *sātireka*, meaning excessive and unbearable. In this context, the teaching stands in the place of the sun’s radiance, and the Blessed One is like the time of the heat.
And by the expression "it blazes intensely," the state of being excessively unbearable is indeed indicated.
In the section on meters (*vṛttapakṣa*), within the *uṣṇih* class of seven-syllable meters, there is an addition.
The rule "ending with the upward-moving [syllable] is *uṣṇih*" is the governing heading (*adhikāra*).
In the *Padyālaṃkāra*, the mention of "*uṣṇihaṃ*" in the plural when not denoting a genus (*ajātau*) is for the purpose of indicating that the final syllable must be heavy (*guru*).
But here, however, because of the context of even meters (*samavṛtta*) and the association with other feet, the status of being heavy (*gurutva*) is appropriate.
"Even though they bestow," and so forth.
Even as she displays the playful charms of a youth to her heart's content, your body, O Jina, possesses the very grace of a youth. 14.
Even while your body assumes the playful movements of a child, it remains exceedingly and utterly graceful and captivating.
O Kumāra among the Jinas!
Indeed, in this world, childish frolics that are not preceded by careful deliberation do not bring satisfaction when observed.
But as for you, even though your body bears those [marks], it is pleasing; this is an apparent contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*).
The resolution [of the contradiction] arises from its dependence on that [subject], namely the disciples (*vineya*), in accordance with their needs.
In terms of meter, in the *uṣṇih* class, this is named *kumāralalitā*.
"It is born," and so forth.
Even for one who merely recollects it, there arises from the multitude of beings a form that has shaken off the nature of the day and ascends upwards. (15)
For the multitude of people who recollect and meditate upon that form of yours,
a state arises— such that their lower nature, consisting of inferiority regarding birth, qualities, and so forth, is completely shaken off, utterly cleansed, and destroyed;
and this occurs not only [in this life].
But rather, it is "upward-moving" (ūrdhvagāmin) because its very nature is to ascend through qualities such as birth and so forth; that is to say, it abides in an exalted state.
In the case of the *vṛtta* meters, the *uṣṇih* is an upward-moving meter;
for others, it is called "exalted" (*uddhatā*).
Furthermore, he describes what that body is like with the words beginning "yadguṇa" (of which the qualities...).

Because the expansion of the praise of his qualities causes attachment to cease, those who have risen above [worldly existence] utter this one steady verse in the *anuṣṭubh* meter as the supreme word. (16)

Because they expand—that is, they propagate—the praise of the qualities of that body in such a way that it is free from attachment (asta-saṅga), meaning devoid of clinging to self-interest; who are these people? They say, they proclaim, that he is wise, learned, one, and without a second.
Who are they?
They have ascended to, that is, attained, the supreme and most excellent state;
this refers to the Buddhas.
Regarding what object they proclaim their steadfastness, he says:
In *anuṣṭubh*:
[the root] *ṣṭubh* means "to obstruct.
Because it has multiple meanings, here it has the sense of "praising."
The *anuṣṭubh* meter is appropriate for the praise (*stobhana*).
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule "after a prefix, before the root *su*" (*upasargāt sunoti*), and so forth.

The meaning is that the Lords of Sages designate as "wise" only that person who, regardless of their own happiness, extends praises of the subtle qualities of Mañjughoṣa; such a one is the one fit for the performance of suitable praise.
Alternatively, "free from the eight attachments" (*asta-saṅgam*) is in apposition either with "the wise one" (*dhīram*) or with the word "foot" (*padam*).
In the section on *vṛtta* meters, regarding the *anuṣṭubh*—the meter consisting of eight syllables—the name "uttama" (supreme) applies.
The governing rule for *anuṣṭubh* extends as far as the *citrapadā*.
Furthermore, he describes what her body is like with the words beginning "ghora" and so forth.
For one whose intellect and vision were obstructed by the terrible darkness of ignorance,
she was like a gem-staffed lamp for all people.
That body of yours, which was a jeweled staff, became a lamp; it became common to the people—meaning it became shared by all. (The suffix -cv- is used here.)
Of what kind of person?
Of one who is *tāmasa*, that is, characterized by darkness (*tamas*).
Delusion itself is *tāmasa* because it obstructs the vision of reality.
He whose eye of wisdom is obstructed by that terrible darkness of delusion.
In the case of the Vṛtta variety of Anuṣṭubh, it is called Samānī.
"O Leader of the World," and so forth.

O Lord of all leaders, even though she is the authoritative means of knowledge for everything, she alone shines forth for us toward that sovereignty of the Lord of Sages which transcends all others in the world. 18.
Furthermore, O Lord of all!

That very body of yours, described in the aforementioned manner, is our *pramāṇikā*—that is, it acts as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for us, providing correct knowledge (*pramiti*), and thus serves as a definitive discernment (*paricchedikā*).
With respect to what is it a means of valid cognition?
Regarding the supreme attainment of the Lords of Sages, which is characterized by the nature of surpassing and transcending the world, he asks:
"What is it like? and says: "It is shimmering," that is, radiant.
For indeed, every means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is a determiner of its object of cognition (*prameya*) precisely by manifesting itself;
likewise, the body of the Blessed One, shimmering all around with the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*), is the determiner of the excellence of the Lord of Sages.
This is according to the maxim: "Where there is form, there qualities abide."
In the *vṛtta* class, within the *anuṣṭubh* meter, there is the *pramāṇikā*.
"Intense," and so forth.
In this lineage of the Perfectly Awakened Ones, which is powerful in its burning away and destruction of intense afflictions,
this [work] of yours bears an ornamentation that shines like a garland of lightning in a cloud.
This body of yours shines; being radiant, it assumes—indeed, performs—the adornment of ornaments.
Where?
In the lineage of the perfectly awakened ones (saṃbuddha).
Of what nature? It is the total destruction of that intense burning, the scorching produced by the afflictions (kleśa).
In this context, "praudhe" means bold. To explain what it is that shines there, he says:
"like a garland of lightning," meaning a wreath of *saudāmanī* flashes.
"Ambhoda" means a water-giver (cloud).
"Tīvra" means intense suffering, affliction, scorching, and burning.
"Prada" refers to the destruction of those two.
Even with the Mañjunātha body, there is a resemblance to a flashing garland of lightning.
In the *anuṣṭubh* meter, when the feet are arranged as described, it is the *vidyunmālā*.
"Ketana-daṇḍam," and so forth.
The playful activity of you, the true Guru, shines forth as if to instruct the world— this young student— in the science of ethics, while holding the staff of the *ketana* tree.
The play and the activity of the true guru shine forth from you, Mañjuśrī. Of what kind [of guru]?

The *ketana* is the sign, the blue lotus (*utpala*); because it possesses a stalk, it is like a staff (*daṇḍa*), and thus "bearing that" is a qualifying attribute used as a reason. For what purpose? To treat the world itself as if it were a young student (*māṇavaka*).
A *māṇavaka* is a youth, a student, or a child.
To teach—that is, to cause him to study—the principles of Dharma;
for a teacher indeed instructs while wielding a rod as a means of instilling fear in students who lack diligence.
In the *anuṣṭubh* meter with the *vṛtta* variety of *pakṣa*, it is the *māṇavaka*.
"Of the three worlds," and so forth.
The palm of your hand, with its trembling sprout-like fingers, rivals the vast expanse of the three worlds as you, O one of great intellect, manifest your own movement throughout them.
The palm of your hand, O one of vast intellect, is like the surface of the earth;
it rivals a swaying young leaf.
The meaning is "in that same way.
Of what kind [of world]?
Of the three worlds, that is, the triple realm (*traidhātuka*).
As he proclaims— meaning reveals— his own destiny among gods and other realms, cast forth by his own auspicious and inauspicious karma,

or his own inherent nature, during the occasion of teaching the Dharma, a similarity is stated to the swaying leaf through the movement of his hand, which manifests the expression of the internal state.
In the *anuṣṭubh* meter, when the feet are even, it is called *kisalaya*.
"Accomplishment," and so forth.
O Supreme Lord of the Universe, your speech, with its variegated words, simultaneously brings about the attainment of the essence of reality within the diverse wonders of the world.
O Lord, your speech is Bhāratī;

being such that it possesses various and manifold words, it simultaneously and at one and the same time brings about the realization—that is, the penetration—of the truth regarding the flavors, namely the supreme ultimate flavor, for the entire world of disciples. That this is so is wonderful and marvelous.
Indeed, although the speech of the Blessed One is non-different, it appears as various words and syllables—assuming diverse forms according to the different dispositions of those to be trained.
In the Vṛtta section, Citrapadā is [defined] in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
"In the Bṛhatī," and so forth.
In her vast and magnificent splendor, some attain the state of being her footstep,
wherein even a sidelong glance from her— once its mark is found— finds rest for a moment.
In whomsoever, in whatever [circumstances],
those [glances] of yours— [even] a sidelong glance, being one that has attained its mark.
Not merely through words and the like, but for a moment they find rest; they truly rest.

Those very few, purified by the falling glance of your eye, attain a firm footing—meaning they gain a stable foundation—in the vast and great prosperity of the fortune of a universal monarch and so forth.
In the *vṛttapakṣa* (metrical section), within the *bṛhatī* meter consisting of nine syllables, there is a novel [meter] named *kaṭākṣa*.
The phrase "in the *bṛhatī*" governs the section up to the end of the *mudrā*.
[The verse begins with: *tvaṃ ṛśaiva*, etc.
Only through contact with one such as you has this [world] attained the state of being worthy;
it shines like the earth when it is continuously ploughed by the tips of the plow.
Moreover, through the very act of being rubbed by your eye— that is, through the cause of familiarity—
this multitude of people,
having attained a state of auspiciousness, meaning becoming worthy vessels for the fruit of peace, shines like a field constantly tilled by the plowshare.

The meaning is as follows: just as the face of a ploughshare is applied continuously and without interruption, so too is the people of such a nature; for just as the earth, when constantly struck by the face of the plough, becomes fit for the production of future fruits, so it is with the people described in that manner.
In the *vṛtta* class, within the *bṛhatī*, there is the *halamukī*.
"Is it not so, Blessed One, that [the earth] is capable of producing the desired fruit for people merely by the removal of its impurities?
For indeed, even the earth is not perceived to be a cause for the abundance of crops merely through the preparation of the plow, in the absence of watering, sowing of seeds, and so forth.
Therefore, how is its fitness (bhavyatā) understood? To this, he says:
"O Giver of Boons," and so forth.
O Giver of Boons, for that transformation is indeed brought about by you;
since the seed of speech sown by you bears fruit in the form of peace within her. (25)
O Giver of Boons!

By such a glance as yours, when it has been cast [upon her], she attains a certain extraordinary transformation—a state of a distinguished self-existence—due to the accumulation of merit gathered over successive cycles of creation, just as the earth [attains excellence] through the watering of its paths and so forth;
for this is indeed so.
It is produced— that is, it is brought to completion— by way of a continuous succession,
because of this series of transformations within this generation.
Having ascertained your capacity, you have sown the very seed that is speech;
peace, which is the subsiding of afflictions, is its characteristic fruit, and it bears— that is, it brings to completion—
just like a seed sown in ground prepared by the application of water and other means.
In the *vṛtta* category, within the *bṛhatī*, it is called *rūpa*.
"To grasp," and so forth.
O Lord, who indeed is capable of comprehending your deeds here, which are like the tracks left by a young serpent in the water during a time of thick darkness? (26)
O Lord!
In this world, indeed, who—being one of limited vision—is capable or able to comprehend and know Your deeds?
Where, what, and how? To this He says:
In a time of dense darkness and thick gloom,
just as the movements of a young serpent are not perceived,
nor even the slithering of a full-grown snake in the water, much less those of its offspring.
Even there, at that time of total darkness;
and thus, the meaning is "your deeds [were performed] in such a manner."
In the *vṛtta* section, within the *bṛhatī* meter, there is the *bhujagaśiśusṛtā*.
He says, beginning with "But nevertheless" (kiṃtu), that even for one such as you, silence alone is appropriate due to a lack of familiarity with the deeds of the Blessed One.
But, O Lord, the joy born from hearing of your fame— which destroys the pride of the world— is now waning,
as the world’s facial expression has been fixed by its own realization of your majesty.
Nevertheless, O Lord, the hearing— that is, the act of listening— to Your fame;
the joy arising therefrom is the delight experienced by the world, that is, by people such as myself.
He casts away—that is, discards—the seal of silence regarding the sphere of conduct.
Of what kind [is this seal]? It belongs to himself, to his own self.
*Prāudhi* means boldness. By the realization of that [boldness], she was placed—that is, established—[in him].

If he, through self-knowledge, has realized his own boldness, thinking "I am not capable in this matter," then for him who remains established in fortitude, how could even his bliss be able to cause a smile upon the seal of his face?
Thus he says: "The destroyer of fortitude."
But in the case of the *vṛtta* meter, it is called *bṛhatī-mudrā*.
"Śrī" and so forth.
O Abode of Fortune, your body, which is skillful in divine play and has reached the further shore of knowledge and conduct,
shines in the assembly of the sons of the Buddha like a lotus among blue water-lilies.
He is addressed again as the one whose dwelling is the abode of splendors; furthermore,
he is the one by whom the further shore— the limit— has been reached and attained.
Of whom?
Of those who possess knowledge and conduct;
"knowledge and conduct" refers to the Noble Eightfold Path.
Right view is knowledge (*vidyā*), while the remaining factors are the conduct (*caraṇa*). For one who does not see or lacks conduct is not capable of proceeding.
Alternatively, the three trainings are knowledge and conduct.
The training in higher wisdom is *vidyā* (knowledge);
the trainings in higher ethical conduct and higher mind are the *caraṇas* (feet).
Because wisdom is of the nature of prior preparation, it is called *caraṇa* (foot) again by virtue of being a "foot"; however, knowledge (*vidyā*) is mentioned first.
Through the purification of that [knowledge], there is the purification of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

For, seeing by means of the eye of wisdom (*prajñācakṣus*) alone, one proceeds by means of those two—ethical discipline and meditative concentration—as if by feet, and thus reaches the destination; it is in this sense that the three trainings (*śikṣā*) are indicated by the term "knowledge and conduct" (*vidyācaraṇa*).
Your *varṣma* is your physical form (*vapuḥ*).
He shines in the assembly circle within the row of the sons of the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas.
Of what nature is he?
He is skillful and captivating through his playful grace.
He explains where, how, and what appears:
"Just as among the lotuses—such as the *kumuda* and *utpala*—there is the *aravinda*, the great lotus.

By this, the superiority of the body of Noble Mañjuśrī over other bodhisattvas is stated, owing to its being the abode of glory (*śrīniketa*) and his having reached the further shore of knowledge and conduct (*vidyācaraṇapāra*), and thus his form being playful and skillful.
Because it is the abode of Śrī and because of its cleverness in playful sport, the superiority of the lotus over other water-born flowers is indeed manifest.
In the case of the *vṛtta* (metrical) variety, within the ten-syllable *paṅkti* meter, there is an unprecedented form named *aravinda*.
"At the end of four" means *caturanta*;
therein, *līlā* refers to a playful variation, that is to say, a specific arrangement of the caesura (*yati*).
The heading "in a row" applies up until the section on the bracelet.
"Tvām," and so forth.

I bow to you, the mountain of the rising of the lineage of the Udgītha, the light of wisdom seated upon the chariot of skillful means, the one exulting in the shattering of dullness, the sun for the lotus-pond of the three worlds. (29)
The syntactical connection is "I revere you.
Of what nature [are you]?
The three worlds constitute the *trailokī*.
By virtue of belonging to the class beginning with *cāturvarṇya*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied; in the feminine, the suffix *ṅīṣ*—characterized by the marker *ṣ*—is added, as in the word *sāmagrī*.
That very [goddess] is Nalinī.
She is the "Producer" (*savitṛ*) of that [Nalinī], just like the sun (*savitṛ*), because she is its illuminator.
That renowned family which is celebrated as the lineage of Bodhisattvas or the lineage of Brahmins and others—
it is in that very [lineage] that he manifests his birth for the sake of others, like the mountain of sunrise.
"Light" means a ray. One whose light is wisdom itself;
"skillful means" for Bodhisattvas consists of many varieties, such as the intention not to abandon any sentient being.

That very chariot is so called because it serves as the means for dispelling the fatigue of wandering in saṃsāra. As it has been said: "Having obtained the Bodhisattva-chariot, which removes all suffering and exhaustion, what conscious person would despair while thus proceeding from happiness to happiness?"
Thus, having expressed the similarity with the sun through the ornament of metaphor (*rūpaka*), the Blessed One’s perfection of his own welfare (*svārthasaṃpat*) has been demonstrated. Now,
making known his perfection of the welfare of others (*parārthasaṃpat*), he says:
Inertness is the ignorance of the world;
he is preeminent in its refutation,
and thus skilled (śauṇḍa) therein.
In the solar context, *jāḍyam* means coldness.
In the row of the square section, there is a lotus;
this too is unprecedented.
"Buddha," and so forth.
O Lord, the splendor of the Buddhas’ sons shines forth intensely through your prosperity,
like the golden summit of a particular mountain, radiant with the luster of jewel-sprouts.
O Lord!

The stages beginning with *muditā* (the Joyous), which are characterized by the state of specific types of knowledge and serve as the vast foundation for the excellence of the qualities of the Bodhisattvas' spiritual preeminence,
shine forth exceedingly and intensely through the perfection of your virtues.

To whom, how, what, by what means, and in what manner does it appear? He says: like gold—that is, like the golden peaks of Sumeru, a particular mountain, which shine exceedingly with the luster of jewel-sprouts.
It is just like that.
In the view of Vṛttapakṣa, this is *paṅkti* called *Rūkmavatī*;
according to some, it is *campakamālā*.
"Without remainder," and so forth.
O Lord, the multitude of the virtuous wanders about with joy, spreading the sound of Your complete victory and illuminating the world, like a drum that proclaims Your fame in every direction. (31)
"Bhuvanodyota" and "Svāmin" constitute the two forms of address.
Just as a proclamation drum, spreading the word of victory for a king or similar authority, is rolled about everywhere, so too does the community of poets act like a proclamation drum for you.
The remainder is easily understood.
In the *vṛttapakṣa* meter, the *paṅkti* consists of five syllables.
"Vāītyādi" (and so forth).
O wise one, through the union with the honey of the virtues of you, the crown jewel of the foremost among the hosts of disputants,
the speech of the three worlds, like a woman intoxicated, sports about, bringing delight even to the steadfast.
The lotus-head of those who are the most eminent and excellent among the multitudes of disputants; or,
the lotus-head of the most eminent [disputant] among the multitudes of disputants.
The head is like his own lotus, because it serves as an ornament by virtue of its excellence.
"You should be addressed as 'O Crown Jewel' (Śiromaṇivat).
Your virtues alone are many, O Śrīdhāman.

Through connection with them—both by association and by being their designator—the Speech of the Three Worlds itself, being intoxicated, shines forth, making even the wise exhilarated and filled with longing, even though they are otherwise devoid of effort in proclaiming your virtues."
Even for the lotus, the abode of Śrī, the garland of bees and other insects becomes intoxicated through contact with honey; thus, it shines forth, exhilarating even the steadfast.
In the case of the *vṛtta* class, when there is a row of eight syllables, it is called *mattā*.
"Viśva," and so forth.
O ornament of the lineage of the Victors who are universal wheel-turners, that state known as "boyhood," which is compared to a peacock’s tail-feathers, clearly withers away in you. (33)

Furthermore, that well-known reputation for "boyhood" (*kumāratā*) which is clearly and manifestly attributed to Kārttikeya— whose very nature it is to be followed by the peacock— is, as it were, fading away now that you, a prince who adorn the lineage of the Victors (*jināḥ*), the sovereigns of the universal wheel, have become a prince who adorns the lineages of many world-system emperors (*trailokyacakravartin*). For you are a prince who serves as the ornament of the lineages of numerous lords of the three worlds.
And that [status] belongs to Śambhu alone, the sole lord of the desire realm;
therefore, the meaning is that his title of "Kumāra" (Prince) seems to wither away in you.
In the *vṛttapakṣa* class, the *mayūrasāriṇī* occurs in the *paṅkti* meter.
"Not so," and so forth.
The series of ornaments upon each limb of yours, garlanded with rays from various jewels, has attained the state of pure white brilliance through the excellence of its own blossoming luster.
Your series of ornaments has been brought to defeat;
what kind [of series]?
It is one that possesses garlands of rays from various jewels.
The suffix *ini* is applied according to the rule for the *vrīhy-ādi* group. By what?
By that abundance of splendor which manifests in every limb and belongs to the state of a fresh maiden.
The address "O Śuddhavirāṭ" is used in the sense of a reason: you shine forth preeminently (*virāṭ*), because you are pure (*śuddha*) and devoid of ornaments, yet you shine forth preeminently.
In the case of the *vṛtta* class, it is *śuddhavirāṭ* when there is a sequence of five [short syllables].
"May he protect," and so forth.

O Lord of Debaters, may your hand protect the world as it gestures during the exposition of the method of reality—its bangles jingling melodiously from the vigorous striking against [the opponent's arguments]. 35.
O Lord of Disputants! May the slight movement, the trembling of your hands, protect the world.
Where is that? He says: [it is here].
At the time of providing an exposition of the system of reality, the path of ultimate truth—
of what nature is it?
It is characterized by mutual contact through the binding of the seal of interpretation by means of thorough integration.
Where there is a bracelet with a tinkling sound and moving bangles.
In the case of the *vṛtta* meter, a ring (*valaya*) consisting of five *paṅkti*s is indeed unprecedented.
"Form," and so forth.

Beholding your form, your multitude of virtues, and your fame— all of which surpass this entire world— the Triṣṭubh meter, having conceived a longing for its own domain, has become slow in producing the universe.

"Having beheld this entire form of yours as surpassing [all others]..."—here, the word *atha* (then/now) is for the purpose of connecting with each term individually, meaning "this entire [form] is surpassing. Thus, it means: "having beheld this multitude of qualities which is entirely surpassing, and likewise having beheld this fame which is entirely surpassing."
Bearing a lack of interest— thinking, "Fie upon our own form and so forth"— toward the matter of the world's perception of his own form, qualities, and fame,
he performs the praise (*stuti*) of his own threefold form, qualities, and fame; [the *ṣ* in *suṣāmā*] is due to the rule regarding the *suṣāmādi* group.
In that [state], a mild [feeling] has arisen.
In the case of the *vṛtta* meter, within the eleven-syllable *triṣṭubh* metre, that which bears a pause at the fifth position is called *upajāti*.
There are five such positions,
and by them, the fifth place is indicated.
The same should be understood for what follows hereafter.
In the fifth [chapter], the meaning is "caesura.

Prior to this, for the previously mentioned meters, the caesura is established by general rule (*utsarga*) at the end of the quarter-verse (*pāda*) alone, because there is no specific injunction (*viśeṣavidhāna*) to the contrary.
From this point until the end of the chapter, this rule applies everywhere;
however, we shall explain the exceptions in their specific contexts.
The governing heading "in the Triṣṭubh" extends as far as the Upajāti meters.
"Tanuḥ," and so forth.
O Lord, whose body shines with a continuous stream of incomparable luster like molten gold, who would not experience joy at the sight of you, O Samantabhadra? (37)
O Lord!
Your body is entirely auspicious and beautiful; for whom, indeed, would such a form not produce joy? The meaning is that it produces joy for everyone.
What kind [of radiance] is it?
It is such that its likeness is the liquid of that compassion which is bodiless yet dense; it possesses a continuous stream of beauty that shines forth and is incomparable to anything else.
The meaning is this: the flow of light from the Blessed One’s body, having pervaded the interior of compassion, appears like the liquid of that compassion as it flows outward.
In the case of the *vṛtta* type, when it consists of *triṣṭubh* feet, it is named *bhadrikā*.
"Autumn," and so forth.

This stainless and radiant white [image], possessing a splendor equal to the multitude of rays from the autumnal moon, shines within your heart in the form of a pearl necklace, like a collection of virtues. (38)
Just as the collection—the gathering—of your virtues, such as wisdom and compassion, shines within your heart, so too does this pearl necklace.
Of what nature is this collection of virtues? It is "vṛttā," meaning possessed of good conduct; it is like a pearl necklace because of its association with round pearls.
Likewise, she is cool like the mass of rays belonging to the autumnal moon;
and because she is free from impurity, she is fair and radiant.
In the case of the *vṛtta* category, that which is composed in the *triṣṭubh* meter is named *vṛttā*.
"Being sung," and so forth.

This garland of yours, which possesses the nature of a benevolent mind and proclaims your fame and victory, shines as if with the humming of swarms of bees arriving to welcome it out of greed for its far-reaching fragrance. (39)
Abounding in fragrance, a treasury of honey, and possessing a powder that is exceedingly sweet like the fourfold [elixir],
she bears the beauty of the blue lotus, reclining happily upon its petals, with the playful movements of bees that never cease.
Two verses:
The beauty of your blue lotus shines.
Of what nature is it?

Among *sumanas* flowers, she is most possessed of mind (*manasvatī*) and wise (*manasvinī*). She is that whose fame—the victory or defeat of the *jāti* flower (either the *jāti* species or the *jāti* blossom) which is exalted by qualities such as fragrance—is being sung. She is thus described.
The word "iva" (as if) is used because there is no actual singing [of the song].
By whom is it being sung? He says:
by the humming of the swarms of bees (*alimālā*) who have come as guests (*svāgatāyāḥ*) due to that fragrance which has spread far and wide.
Even though there is mutual dependence, the compound is formed because the meaning is clearly conveyed.
In the case of the *vṛtta* class, *svāgatā* occurs within the *triṣṭubh* meter.
Furthermore, he asks what the beauty of the blue lotus is like and says, "sfārāmoda... and so forth; these two words are self-evident.
She bears an abundant powder, *parāga*;
of what kind? It consists of the four equal parts (*catuḥsama*) of saffron and the other ingredients.
This [description] applies equally to all four;
it should also be applied here to the term "powder" (*cūrṇa*). Alternatively, the connection is with the preceding [phrase]: "it appears as if that were even more."
That in which one lies is a "bed" (śayana).
A "petal" (dala) is a leaf.
That very [leaf] is a pleasant bed.
In that regard, there is lying down comfortably upon a leaf;
by that [means], it is not fully sufficient or complete,
because of the non-cessation of desire.
It is so called because it possesses the playful movements of bees.
In the *vṛtta* (metrical) variety, the *bhramaravilasitā* is composed in the *triṣṭubh* meter.

It consists of four equal syllables; that which arises from them, or that which is equal across four [quarters], is called *cātuḥsama*. Bearing the "crushing" (*cūrṇana*) or "breaking" (*bhaṅga*) [of the rhythm], it is the *bhramaravilasitā*.
And likewise, in the *Padyālaṅkāra*, it is stated: "In the case of a break in a *veda* [meter], it is the *bhramaravilasitā*."
"Form," and so forth.
Through his cultivation of the elixir of beauty, he is to be highly honored as Vāsava himself,
by whom the pair of eyes born from Ambikā were long ago rendered free of blinking and devoid of the intoxication of pride.
Your very form is like an elixir (*rasāyana*) because it is a cause for nourishing the eyes;
[this occurs] through its cultivation, that is, through repeated practice.
The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of either "cause" (*hetu*) or "instrument" (*karaṇa*).
Indra alone is to be honored and praised in such a way that he becomes manifold, or he is honored among many. How is it that he alone is so? He says:
By which Vāsava, or by which means— that is understood as "by that Vāsava"—
the multitude of eyes (*ambakajātam*), meaning the collection of eyes, was obtained, casting away the blinking, that is, becoming unblinking.
Of what nature is it?
For "cirāya" means for a long time. [It is that which] "dhayati"—that is, drinks—this "ada," this elixir of form and flavor; thus, by the rule "āto 'nupasargāt kaḥ," the suffix *ka* is applied.

*Adodham*: with the suffix *kan* in its own sense (*svārthe*), it becomes *adodhaka*. The meaning is that because he drinks the elixir of your form for a long time with his thousand unblinking eyes, therefore Vāsava alone is to be highly honored, and no one else.
In the *vṛtta* (metrical) category, the *dodhaka* consists of three *triṣṭubh* feet.
"By devotion," and so forth.

This pair of your feet has been attended for a very long time by the fortunate ones—those whose hands are joined in *añjali* with jeweled crowns bowed in devotion, who are overjoyed, and who have cast off all other obligations. 42.
By those very people— whose crowns made of jewels were bowed down completely on all sides with devotion,
who had joined their palms in a hollowed gesture like young elephants,
and who were themselves humble— the pair of your feet was long attended and worshipped.
Because others are not fit vessels;
it is free from other rules and has abandoned other tasks.
In the case of the *vṛtta* type, it occurs within a *triṣṭubh* meter.
"What is it? and so forth.
O Lord of the Intellect, what is the use of Indra’s power, or even of Brahmā’s glory, or of any prosperity exceeding them? If [the mind] is established in Your lotus feet, all is fully accomplished.
O Lord of Wisdom, if attendance at Your lotus feet is accomplished, then what need is there for the power and prosperity of Indra? What use is the wealth of Brahmā?
Therefore, what is the use even of the attainment of the formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) and so forth, which surpass those two?
Nothing at all.
The intended meaning is that by means of worshiping your lotus feet, even enlightenment (*bodhi*) is attained.
In the case of the Vṛtta variety, it is established in the Triṣṭubh meter.
"tvad" and so forth.

In this difficult cycle of birth, karma and affliction—both fierce and acting together—will surely lead one who is averse to serving you to destruction, just as wind and waves together destroy a ship in the midst of the ocean. 44.
In this world, birth itself is difficult to transcend;
it renders one helpless and dependent on others—
a person who is averse to your service.
Karma is wholesome and unwholesome;
affliction consists of passion and so forth;
these two, having become intense, combine.
"Exceedingly" (atyartham) means necessarily (avaśyam), by rule (niyamena).
The connection [of these words] is with "they lead to destruction" (nāśaṃ nayataḥ).
What, who, where, and how?
The wind and the wave—those two carry away that ship into the middle of the ocean; thus [is it].
In the case of the meter, within the Triṣṭubh, there is a meter named Vātormī.
Others call it *vātormimālā* and desire the pause (*yati*) at the ocean (four syllables).
Thus says the Omniscient One of the Kali Age: "If there are *ma*, *vā*, or *sra*, it is *vātormimālā*."
Nevertheless, it has been shown here out of regard for the preceding [work], and thus it is a poetic ornament (*padyālaṃkāra*).
"Far away," and so forth.
The mental continuum of those with far-reaching vision, though free from fault, flashes forth in some inexplicable way;
it is stirred by the longing to attend upon you, which has been most incessant since beginningless time.

They are blameless and faultless; for this very reason, their far-seeing minds are most unceasing, because there is not even the slightest interruption. An indescribable mental continuum shines forth with particular intensity.
Of what nature was she?

She was one whose mind was uplifted by the longing for that service to you— the worship of you— which has continued throughout existence, up to the very limit of cyclic rebirth (*ābhavaṃ bhavaparyantam*).
Even while being ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), they perceive what is beneficial for the future and are free from evil in the present.
The meaning is that it is only for them, as described, that the aforementioned mental continuum (*cittasaṃtati*) manifests, and not for others.
In the case of the *vṛtta* (metrical) variety, the *rathoddhatā* is composed in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
"Cutting," and so forth.

Upon the mere glance of your eye, there arises a certain extraordinary state of merit, characterized by mature wisdom, which brings about the swift attainment of the four noble truths—the nectar that puts an end to all delusions. (46)
"Even at the mere glance of your sidelong look, a state of merit arises for people"— this is the ellipsis.
Of what nature is it?
She is endowed with mature wisdom;
for according to the lexicon, "one who possesses *śālī* [grain] is to be known as *śālīna* [modest].
Furthermore, of what nature is she?

It is pleasing when there is the cutting off of the four delusions—the four perversions—which have the nature of grasping at permanence, self, pleasure, and purity within that which is impermanent, non-self, suffering, and impure.
For what purpose is their cutting off? He says:
"Those which are the truths of the Noble Ones."
The characteristics of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are the signs for their swift and rapid attainment.
In the case of the *vṛtta* meter, *śālinī* consists of three *triṣṭubh* feet; it is pleasing when there is a break or pause after the fourth syllable.
"Renown," and so forth.
O you who cause the cessation of suffering, your hymn of praise—swiftly removing all distress—is carried by a multitude of songs;
like pale sandalwood moistened by the thick moonlight of the full moon, it beautifully adorns the ten directions.
*Aratiḥ* is suffering; from its cause comes your *kīrtiḥ* (fame).
*Alam* means excessively;
it ornaments the ten directions.
Of what kind [is he]?
Of one who is the vessel for a collection of hymns—a multitude of praises.
Again, of what kind?
It is called *atisadyanohṛta* because it excessively captivates the minds of the virtuous (*satām*).
Due to its being conceptualized (*vikalpitatvāt*), there is neither the presence nor the absence of the suffix *ñam*.
Of what nature is this fame?
It is thick like the moonlight—the radiance of the moon—and moist like sandalwood; it is "śyenī," meaning white.
This form is derived from the word *śyeta* with the addition of the feminine suffix *ṅī*, and the substitution of *na* for the letter *ta*.
In the case of the *vṛtta* type, the *śyenī* consists of three *triṣṭubh* feet.
"tvad" and so forth.

With its many crests rising high, the mountain form— its view of sentient beings difficult to abandon due to its reliance on you— bows down and follows [you], as if split apart by the blow of Indra’s fierce thunderbolt.
Through reliance upon you, the view of a sentient being (*sattvadṛṣṭi*) and the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), though difficult to abandon, gradually undergoes destruction and passes away.
Of what nature is it? It has risen high with many crests—that is, with twenty peaks.
Just as the form of a mountain, though rising high with many peaks, when struck by the fierce thunderbolt of Indra, goes to utter destruction once it is split apart;
so too is form [regarded as] the self, the self as possessing form, the self as being in form, and form as being in the self.
This applies likewise to feeling and the other aggregates.
Thus, this mountain, lofty with twenty peaks, meets its destruction by the thunderbolt of the knowledge of the Lord’s intention regarding selflessness.
In the case of the *vṛtta* meter, the *indravajrā* is a *triṣṭubh*;
it begins with "virūḍha," and so forth.
Seated upon a lofty lion-throne worthy of the sovereign power of the flourishing Dharma,
you are attended by Śiva, Upendra, Vajrāyudha, and Vedhas, who are themselves lovely and auspicious.
Śivāpati, Upendra, Vajrāyus, and Vedhas—they wait upon you.
Of what nature are they?
They are those for whom the beloved, desired, and auspicious state of Nirvāṇa is their goal; being such as these.

Of what nature were you? You were seated upon a lofty, high lion-throne, which was appropriate and worthy for that majestic sovereignty over the Dharma—the state of being the Lord of Dharma—that had grown and flourished.
In the case of the *vṛtta* class, [the meter] is *upendravajrā* within the *triṣṭubh*.
"Immediately following," and so forth.

May those Upajāti meters of the gods—whose feet consist of the characteristics just described and whose eyes are the elaborate array of *śravyayati*—be within your range of perception; they are truly blessed.
The characteristics that were just mentioned—beginning with "What need for Indra’s splendors?
and so forth—are the essential natures, such as being the cause of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*naiḥśreyasa*).
By means of these, the first two [goals] are accomplished.
And here, "immediate" (*ānantarya*) refers to the absence of any interruption by a similar [state], as in the expression: "Immediately after Vikramāditya, King Śrīharṣa became king.
Alternatively, it is an address to the Blessed One, meaning "one whose characteristics have been manifested immediately [following his enlightenment]."

And by the very marks [such as the wheel] upon your feet, they are worthy of being grasped. Likewise, those two feet of yours— whose gait and restraint are so extensive that even the elaborate cadences of the scriptures and the like are audible, and which are free from all distraction— are such that those species of beings, whether human or otherwise, whose very sight falls within their range are truly blessed.
And it should be understood that they exist in the vicinity (*upa-samīpe*) of the gods;
this is because of their proximity to the state of being gods and so forth.

In the case of the *vṛtta* meter, the first two quarters [of the verse] should possess the characteristics of the *indravajra* and *upendravajra* meters as just described; furthermore, they should have a variety of pleasing pauses (*yati*). In this context, the pause occurs specifically at the end of the quarter, and there should be a "variety" (*prapañca*) because such pauses occur in many instances within each quarter.
Those fourteen *upajāti* meters are to be understood;
this is because of the use of the plural number.
Therefore, there are fourteen varieties of *upajāti* meters among the *triṣṭubh* verses.
Generally, the sūtras here consist of types of summaries from the Śāntisūtra;
however, in some places, even an iṣṭi is not seen at all.
"Without doubt," and so forth.
Without doubt, O Lord of Men, although there are others who fully emulate all your personal qualities,
those who have conquered the god of love desire you as the sole pillar of their lineage because of a devotion that is shared by no other.
Those whose nature it is to emulate to the utmost and in an exceeding degree all the qualities of themselves— that is, of the Bodhisattvas—
or all the qualities of the noble Mañjuśrī himself that are carried by wisdom;
even though other Bodhisattvas exist, [they do so] without doubt and with certainty.

The Buddhas, who are victorious over the bodiless one (Anaṅga), are the lords and protectors of the Bodhisattvas; they desire—that is, they declare—that you alone abide in the lineage, namely, the Buddha-lineage. Thus you are "vaṃśastha" (abiding in the lineage).
They speak thus.
By what? By means of *dhi*, that is, by wisdom (*prajñā*). Of what nature? Unshared with others.
In the section concerning the *vṛtta* meters, the term "triṣṭubh" is excluded,
as the term "jagatī" will be mentioned later.
Therefore, in the *jagatī* meter— that is, in a meter consisting of twelve syllables— the name is *vaṃśastha*.
"Child," and so forth.

O beloved one, I bow to Vāgīśvara, who has the form of a child adorned with various ornaments, who is golden-hued, whose crest is graced by Akṣobhya, and who is the glory arising from the sustenance of the lineage of the Lord of Sages through his personifications as Speech, Intellect, and Form. 52.
"By means of speech, intellect, and form" refers to body, speech, and mind.
This lineage of the lords of sages is the "Maunīndra" (Lord of Sages) lineage;
its glory of prosperity is such that it serves as an ornament for that lineage.
The remainder is easily understood.
In the case of the *jagatī* meter, when the first syllable of *vaṃśastha* itself is heavy, it is called *indravaṃśā*; this is the distinction between these two.
"By means of excessive elaborations," and so forth.

O Lord, even with words of extreme prolixity, those of sweet voice cannot reach the further shore of Your virtues; yet, O Blessed One, this praise of mine, though composed of few syllables, is truly beautiful as it generates nothing but my own joy.
O Adhinātha!
Even with the expansiveness of their speech, those sages of beautiful voice (*sugiraḥ*) have not reached, nor attained, the further shore— the limit— of Your qualities.

He says that, in that case, your praise is indeed inappropriate: "Even such a praise of mine as this, consisting of measured syllables, is auspicious— that is, beautiful— because it brings joy to you, the self of the one who praises."
That very [verse] is "tanmātra" because it has reached the limit of qualities worthy of praise;
it is that by which [the state] is produced.
In the case of prosody, it is the *pramitākṣarā* meter in the *jagatī* class.
"Blazing," and so forth.
O Lord of Bharati, the Goddess of Speech— adorned with all glittering ornaments, having attained her rise from the lotus-faces of the meritorious,
radiant by her very nature, and garlanded with excellent virtues— approaches you of her own accord.
O Lord of Bhāratī!
Bhāratī herself—Sarasvatī herself—approaches and takes refuge in you at your svayaṃvara.
Of what nature is she?
The garland (*sragmālā*) consists of those very virtues of the Blessed One which are radiant by their own nature and devoid of all defects;
she is the one who possesses this as her subject matter (*abhidheyatva*).
The suffix *vini* is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) after the word *sraj*.
Likewise, she possesses glory (*śrī*) through all those ornaments that shine brightly—the poetic ornaments (*kāvyālaṅkṛti*);
the suffix *ini* is applied here according to the rule for the *vrīhy-ādi* group.
Furthermore, of what nature was she?

She was one whose birth and origin were obtained from the lotus-face of the Bodhisattvas who possess merit; and though she was Sarasvatī herself, she was adorned with the splendor of all her radiant ornaments.
By nature, she was also resplendent, having obtained her origin from the lotus-face of the Brahmas who possess merit.
This is because of the statement, "Sarasvatī is entirely white.
She is *sragviṇī*, meaning she possesses a garland (*srak*) consisting of a beautiful (*san*) and excellent (*śobhana*) thread (*guṇa*).
Alternatively, the meaning is that she herself approaches you, having abandoned the Lord of Śrī (Viṣṇu).
In the Jagatī meter, when the feet consist of four syllables each, it is the Sragviṇī.
"Disintegration," and so forth.
The arrows of the five-arrowed one have been brought to ruin; the fire of hatred has been extinguished, and the dullness born of delusion has been cast away.
O Lord, whose form is intent upon bestowing grace upon the three worlds, the prosperity of the Viśvedevas has indeed been attained by you alone.
O Lord!
This prosperity, which belongs to the Viśvedevas—both they and the universe being yours—is indeed attained by you alone and by no one else.
He asks: "How so? and says:
Since the arrows of the five-arrowed one (Kāma) were brought to ruin and destroyed by you,
this declares your victory over desire;
likewise, the fire of hatred has been extinguished by you.
Why?
Because the form "śānta" (pacified) contains an implied causative sense (*ṇyartha*),
and thus the dullness born of delusion is eliminated.
And here, even without that [word], the meaning is obtained;
yet by Śambhu, desire alone was conquered,
and by Brahmā, hatred.
The sun possesses dullness;
however, the distinction is that you have attained the perfection of all these qualities.
The epithet "one whose form is intent upon blessing the three worlds" is used as a reason for this distinction.
For that which is not established for oneself cannot be intended to prove something for another.

Alternatively, he says "trailokya... and so forth, meaning: if passion and the like have been abandoned by the Blessed One, then there would be a loss of the welfare of the sentient beings you hold dear.
By this, his remaining in the world of existence (*bhava*) out of compassion is indicated.
In the case of the meter, it is *vaiśvadevī* in the world;
the five arrows (*bāṇa*) therein have been brought to a break (*bhaṅga*).
"Complete," and so forth.
Filled with the various jewels of internal virtues, you, O steadfast one, through your great fortitude,
bear the grace of a garland of clouds with the showers of the true Dharma’s rain— streams that extinguish the fire of afflictions.
Those qualities which are contained within are themselves the jewels;
it is filled with those various and manifold wonders,
or rather, with the jewels that are the multitude of its qualities.
Being completely full within,
you maintain the restraint (*yati*)— that is, the disciplined conduct— of the ocean (*ambhorāśi*) due to your extreme fortitude;
likewise, it should be understood that you maintain the grace (*līlā*) of a garland of clouds.
By what? It is the fire of affliction itself that it pacifies,
or by means of which [it] is thoroughly pacified.
That very stream of the rain of the True Dharma, together with its winds,
[is like] an ocean filled with various jewels and exceedingly steadfast;
likewise, a mass of clouds also extinguishes fire with its torrential downpour— such is the similarity.

In the case of the *vṛtta* meter, one should connect the passage as follows: "The row of clouds bears [the likeness] of a mass of water in the *jagatī* meter, which possesses a pause (*yati*) within the ocean.
Regarding the words "of you" (*tava*), and so forth...
In your presence, opponents who are otherwise esteemed as supreme and skilled become overwhelmed by fear; they consider even a few words spoken in rapid or slow cadence to be a state of easy silence.

O Supreme One! Even those such as Bṛhaspati and others, who are considered by you to be the most excellent among opponents, are [surpassed]; or "Paramottama" may be taken as an address: "O You who are esteemed as the most excellent.
Those who are regarded as supreme—[to them You are superior].
Whether spoken quickly or slowly, whatever word is uttered as a qualifier of an action or of speech itself—
that too they hold in high regard.
Of what nature are they?
They are those for whom the state of being mute is easily attained.
How is it that they are so? He says:
They are deficient in brilliant intuition;
for those devoid of intuition, silence alone is appropriate.
Yet even they, if they utter speech—whether rapidly or slowly—[are to be understood as such].
Then, they value even that highly according to the maxim that "the strength of a tree is better than death.
In the case of the *vṛtta* (meter), it is *drutavilambita* in the *jagatī* [meter].
"Regarding the phrase beginning with 'tritaya'... [and so forth].
Purifying all three worlds with a radiance as white as the rays of the moon,
your fame endures for a long time, just as the Mandākinī flows eternally from the summit of the celestial mountain.
Your fame arises, purifying all three worlds;
and from the summit of the divine mountain, the celestial river Mandākinī arises. That [river], bestowing luster, arises upon the peak of Mount Meru.
The word *mandākinī* is recited [in lexicons] as the name for the celestial river;
yet, even though it is so recited, it is seen in poetic convention as the river that flows through the three paths (*tripathagā*).
Therefore, it is said that she purifies all three.
Of what nature are they?
Your fame and the Mandākinī are both such that their luster is as pure as the rays of the moon.
And because the Blessed One has the luster of gold, there is a similarity with the peak of Mount Meru.
In the Jagatī meter, when the *vṛtta* (syllabic) variety is used, it is called Mandākinī.
"He takes," and so forth.
O Abode of Compassion, this fame of yours, which captivates the hearts of those whose minds are devoted to your deeds,
utterly carries away [all else] in every direction, like a blossoming jasmine creeper covering the ground on all sides with its mass of flowers.
Just as the *kundalatā* creeper is completely covered and pervaded on all sides by a mass of blossoms— a profusion of flowers—
it utterly captivates the hearts of the wise, those who have performed meritorious deeds, in every direction.
Likewise, O abode of compassion!
This fame of yours, just described, spreading in every direction throughout all quarters, utterly captivates the hearts of the wise.
In the Jagatī meter, under the category of Vṛtta, there is an unprecedented [meter] named Kunda-latā.
"It causes to fall," and so forth.
This certain ocean of compassion, who gathers together the accumulated splendor of the world and dispels the sins of all beings,
is skilled in manifesting many millions of Buddhas and maintains the playful sovereignty of the Lord of Speech within the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
He who has assumed the playful sport of the Buddha, the Lord of Speech of the Dharmadhātu—he is this certain ocean of compassion.
He shatters the sins and evils of the worlds.
Of what nature is he?
One by whom a collection of splendors has been acquired and amassed;
one who is exceedingly capable— that is, extremely competent— in the manifestation, radiation, or generation of many millions of Buddhas.
It is so designated because of the emanation of many millions of Buddhas from the body of Noble Mañjuśrī, and because they manifest through his propitiation.

In the *vṛtta* variety, it consists of half a *dala* (petal) for each foot; it is characterized by a beautiful arrangement of pauses (*yati*) as they occur therein, and its name, *Vāgīśvaralīla*, is unprecedented in the world.
"He scatters," and so forth.
Scattering as it were heaps of radiant luster— the brilliance of the tremulous waves of the celestial river—
your sword, dark as the waters of the Yamunā, shines eternally within the edge of its blade.
While you eternally sport within another form in the midst of your own cosmic state, amidst the *Arapacana* syllabary and other manifestations,
your sword— dark blue like the ripples of the Yamunā’s water—
seems to scatter and sprinkle the masses of radiance from your very body with its own intense brilliance.
Of what sort?
Of those whose color and luster are like the shimmering waves of the celestial river (the Milky Way), because they too possess clarity and are both broken and spread out.
By this, a similarity to the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is demonstrated.

Alternatively, the construction is as follows: when you scatter heaps of the aforementioned splendors within the interval of your own state (*daśā*), the sword, possessing the qualities described therein, shines eternally right there.
In the Jagatī meter, in the even pādas, there is [a pause] named Yamunā.
"Mind," and so forth.
O Lord, sovereign of all beauty, where is this form of yours, so charming with its captivating strings of pearls?
And where is that terrifying gait like a serpent, which glows for the sake of pacifying even the most uncontrollable beings? (62)
"O Lord!
How charming is this form of yours, beautiful with a captivating necklace!

By the address "Sovereign of the Beautiful," [the author] demonstrates that the King assumed such royal deportment and the like for the purpose of humbling those who pride themselves on their own beauty.

The meaning is that two forms of yours are exceedingly marvelous: one is the form of Yama and others, which is resorted to by serpents—fierce, terrifying, and moving—that manifest for the sake of pacifying beings who are difficult to subdue; and [the other] is for the sake of ornamentation. Thus, there are two forms of yours that cause great wonder.
In the Jagatī meter, the Vṛttapakṣa variety is the Bhujaṅgaprayāta.
"Uninterrupted," and so forth.

O Lord, whose mind is not captivated by this form of yours, adorned with a profusion of closely-set pearls, which resembles a fresh garland of beautiful jasmine flowers fit for seasonal enjoyment? 63.
O Lord!

That form of yours possesses a fresh and newly made garland—indeed, a most beautiful jasmine garland—that is to be worn during the season of youth; or rather, it is that form which possesses a fresh garland of jasmine itself, fit to be worn at the time when the jasmine is in full bloom.
This very form of yours—whose mind does it not captivate?
The meaning is that it captivates everyone.
Of what nature is it?
By means of a dense mass of pearls;
or she whose very ground is that [mass] itself.
In the Jagatī meter, when the feet consist of [the sequence] vṛtta-pakṣa, it is called Navamālinī.
"Your," and so forth.

O Lord, if the eye of the world, greedy to behold your auspicious form, were to wander all around with a "jhāṭ" sound as it exhausts itself in the ocean of the nectar of your supreme splendor, [it would find no rest]. (64)
The word *aṅga* is used as a term of address:
"O Lord! O Protector, the very luster of your eyes for the world is an ocean of nectar; in that [ocean], the supreme exhaustion of fatigue is cast off with a splashing sound.
Not otherwise;
for even the ocean resounds with the *zhātkāra* sound through the succession of its tides,
and the Blessed One likewise [resounds] with the waves of his ceaseless and eternal beauty.
Of what nature is the eye of the world?
It is "lampaṭaka," meaning it wanders (*aṭati*) everywhere (*paritaḥ*, *samantāt*) intent upon the observation of that beautiful and captivating form;
thus, it is itself a wanderer (*aṭaka*).
For this very reason, he undergoes this exertion;
for even another person, exhausted by long wandering, dispels his fatigue at a great body of water such as the ocean.
In the Jagatī meter, when the number of syllables per quarter-verse is sixteen, it is the Toṭaka.
"O Giver of Boons," and so forth.
O Giver of Boons, O Transcender of Existence, our limbs shall certainly manifest the state of renunciation;
this pair of ear-cavities, a vessel for drinking the nectar of your words, shall surely be the cause of our joy. (65)
O Giver of Boons!
O One who has transcended all existence!
Our limbs—our hands, feet, and so forth.
It is evident that they resort to detachment and lack of interest; the meaning is that [worldly objects] do not become causes of happiness for them.
"The pair of ears" refers to their cavities.
Furthermore, he will certainly be a cause of joy for us.
How so? Because he is a drinking vessel for the nectar of your speech.
In the *jagatī* meter with a rounded wing, there is a form named *puṭa*;
here, the eight constituent parts possess pauses.
"Choose," and so forth.

I choose this boon from you, O one of incomparable power: that a person such as I may not exist for your protection—nor even one who, while taking refuge in you, displays the dull and arrogant conduct of turning away from the nectar-essence of tranquility.
O you of incomparable power!
From you, from your presence, I choose—one boon; I entreat it.
"What boon do you entreat? he asked.
"May no person like me ever arise among you!
Of what sort?
One whose speech, mind, and conduct are dull, sluggish, arrogant, and distracted—even while taking refuge in one such as you, the Lord of Speech."
He becomes one from whom delight and longing have departed;
in what object?
In those very nectars which are the states of tranquility.
In the *jagatī* meter, when the feet consist of seven syllables, there is a variety called *jaloddhatagati*;
in that case, the pause occurs after six syllables.
"Tvad" and so forth.

O Moon, by the power of the merit arising from your grace, the person who creates [this work] attains the bliss that pierces the eightfold coverings; thus, for embodied beings, it becomes the path to the destruction of worldly existence, serving as a festival for the eyes.

O Moon, by the power of that auspiciousness which has arisen and flourished through your grace—grace that brings about a festival for the eyes of embodied beings and bestows delight upon their vision—the man of action effortlessly attains the path of the noble ones, the way that shatters worldly existence. Of what nature is that path? It is the very path of bliss.
It is eightfold;
it is characterized by the noble eightfold path.
In the case of the *vṛtta* (metrical) *jagatī*, there is that which is called *candravartman*;
it has eight divisions, meaning it consists of eight *yati*s (caesuras).
"Bliss," and so forth.

O King of Debaters, those fortunate ones whose memory remains unimpaired even by the various causes such as the extremes of pleasure and pain, possess the essence of wisdom obtained by taking refuge at your feet throughout every course of existence.

He is the King of Speakers (Vādirāja). Those for whom memory is unimpaired— despite being born from the causes of pleasure, pain, their intensities, and those things beginning with pleasure— are the fortunate ones (bhavya).
Even when existing within all states of existence, such as those of gods and others, they remain the same.
Now, one might object: "The world, having encountered causes for unsurpassed happiness and so forth, becomes one whose memory is lost;
how then can this be said? To this, he says:
Because those who have obtained the essence and strength of intelligence by taking refuge at your feet are such as you have described;
or else, because [they have obtained it] in the entire course of all kings of disputants— that is, in all legal proceedings involving controversy—
the rest is the same.
In the section on *vṛtta* meters, the term "in the *jagatī*" refers to a new type of *kalā*;
from this point onward, the phrase "in the *jagatī*" does not recur.
"Your," and so forth.
