O you whose mind is honored by virtues of far-reaching renown, arising from the total removal of the veil of all impurities—for those who delight in serving your feet, an indescribable happiness arises in this world in the form of spiritual action. 69.
For those whose delight lies in the service and worship of Your feet, a certain wonderful state of perfection arises in this world as their true nature;
how is it wonderful? He explains:
it is because, through the removal of the entire veil of impurity, their greatness—that is, their vastness—is radiant and illuminating by nature.

"Great intellect" (*mahatī matiḥ*) refers to a particular state of awakening (*avabodha-viśeṣa*) characterized by qualities such as the capacity for speech and so forth; that [state] in which this exists is "possessing great intellect.
Alternatively, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both radiant due to the removal of the entire mass of impurities and honored by the quality of its renown."
In the *vṛttapakṣa* (metrical section), within the *atijagatī* meter consisting of thirteen syllables, there is the name "Mahita."
"Black," and so forth.

May he whose body is as lovely as refined gold, who is served by the excellent female swan of eloquent speech, and who is celebrated here as Mañjughoṣa—the singular royal swan upon the lotus-pond of the Conqueror’s mind—protect you. (70)
In this world, he who is renowned and celebrated as Mañjughoṣa—like a *kalahaṃsa* swan amidst that single, preeminent lotus-pond which is the very mind of the Victorious One—may he protect you.
Of what nature is he? His body is as lovely as *kaladhauta*, that is, gold.
And thus Rabhasa states: "Kaladhauta means gold or silver.
Since she is constantly followed by that clever speech which is itself the female swan (varaṭā) or goose, he is to be served—that is, attended upon—by her.
In this world, even though he is a *haṃsa* (swan) preeminent in his notes within the lotus pond, he is renowned as Mañjughoṣa because his voice is melodious;
he is to be served by a female swan (*varaṭā*) characterized by eloquent speech;
and being of noble conduct, his body becomes pure like refined gold (*kaladhauta*).
In the *vṛttapakṣa* of the *atijagatī* meter, there is a metre named *kalahaṃsa*;
its ancient name is also *bhramarī*.
"Interruption," and so forth.
If there were a severance from these three unbearable afflictions, it would clearly be difficult to do so even in the slightest degree;
for where indeed, O Protector, could such a form be found here in the three worlds that gladdens both the eyes and the mind? (71)
O Lord!
If it were difficult to sever even those [energies] with coarse activity, such a form would not be attained.

If, however, it were impossible to sever—even into atoms—those with subtle activity, then where indeed in these three worlds could such a form of the Blessed One be found? The meaning is that it would not be found at all.
Of what nature is it?
She whose nature (*śīla*) is to delight both the eyes and the mind is "such" (*tathā*).
As it has been said: "O Blessed One, your very form proclaims your freedom from passion," and so forth.
In the *vṛttapakṣa* of the *atijagatī* meter, if there is a pause after the third [syllable], then it is the *praharṣiṇī*.
"In the ocean of milk," and so forth.
If one were to set aside the cessation of waters in the ocean— the repository of jewels consisting of shimmering masses of great rays—
and observe the continuity of luster in the body of one such as you, then this beauty would be truly such [as it appears].
Such a beautiful succession of splendors as this is seen only in the bodies of great Bodhisattvas like you.

If, for a moment, one were to effect the cessation—that is, the disappearance—of water therein, then this [comparison] would be merely imagined, such as: "If both [streams] were separate flows in the sky," and so forth.
In the *vṛtta* section, within the *atijagatī* meter consisting of four quarters, having established the pause at the fourth [syllable], this such beautiful [meter] is observed.
"‘Mandra,’ etc. [refers to the following:]

O Lord, when you, who delight the worthy ones, roar aloud and emit delightful streams of nectar, that very asceticism—which follows the rain-cloud with extreme beauty and clarity—is called *mattamayūra*. 73.
O Lord!

As you, O captivating one, emit high-pitched streams of the sacred teachings—torrents of nectar with deep and resonant sounds—you alone, O delighter of the worthy (bhavya), manifest the conduct of the ascetic;
thus, that very conduct clearly and distinctly follows the rain-cloud of the ascetic.
Because it is exceedingly pleasing to the mind;
because the monsoon clouds, with their deep rumblings, have signaled the release of streams of nectar; and because the peacocks are intoxicated [with joy].
The state of being a worthy recipient, satisfied by the truth.
The pause that was just mentioned for the *rucirā* meter in its *vṛttapakṣa* (syllabic variety) when occurring in the fourth foot, follows as the *mattamayūra* meter in the *atijagatī* class.
"Victorious," and so forth.

This creeper, emerging from the beautiful flower-eyes upon you—who, like the springtime, brings unsurpassed joy to the three worlds—is victorious; it speaks with the sweet sound of bees intoxicated by honey, as if rising from the blue-lotus tree.
In you, the cause of the birth and the progenitor of joy for the three worlds,
there triumphs the creeper— the branch— of the utpala-tree, which is like the springtime (madhu) abiding in the ketaka-lotus tree.
Of what sort is it?
She is one who has arisen from that flower which is beloved by the eyes of the three worlds;
likewise, she is one whose nature it is to speak sweetly with the humming of bees intoxicated by honey.
Furthermore, the season of spring (madhusamaya) also generates joy for the three worlds.

And there, the branch of the blue-lotus tree, shimmering with flowers as lovely as eyes and resonant with the humming of bees intoxicated by drinking its nectar, becomes like a woman speaking enchanting words.
In the *vṛttapakṣa* (metrical section), within the *atijagatī* [meter], this is *mañjubhāṣiṇī*;
however, previously it was named *kusumodgatā*.
For this very reason, both names have been included here.
"All," and so forth.

We consider your conduct alone to be like a fresh mango blossom, adorned with the principles of the Jina and celebrated by swarms of wise bees who have attained joy through being filled with qualities that surpass all others. 75.
Just as the fresh mango blossom is the ornament that adorns spring, we consider your very conduct to be the adornment of the Jina’s doctrine.
Of what nature is it?
It is being sung and celebrated by the swarms of bees, which are none other than the wise.
By what kind [of beings]?
By those who have attained intense joy through those very qualities of yours that surpass all others;

being praised, as it were, by throngs of bards consisting of the families of *mahuvrataka* trees, which have attained intense joy through their own qualities—such as fragrance—that surpass all others, even though they are merely mango trees (*cūta*).
The word *eva* is used in the sense of *iva* (like).
Thus Ajaya states: "The word *eva* [is used] in the sense of comparison (*upamya*) and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*)."
In the section on meters, it will be stated that [this] is the Śakvarī ornament.
"Face-to-face," and so forth.

I bow deeply to that great deity of the assembly of disputants, the root of prosperity, who is mounted upon the back of a lion facing him directly, who is exceedingly compassionate, and whose feet possess a golden luster that is not unevenly beautiful. 76.
I bow down with great intensity to the tutelary deity of the lineage of debaters.
Of what nature is he?

He is one whose face is turned directly toward the Blessed One himself, and who has mounted upon the back of the lord of beasts and serpents, possessing exceedingly profound compassion—that is, a compassion that surpasses all others.
The bulbous root of prosperity and splendor;
likewise, his beauty was such that by it his golden and snow-white feet were rendered beautiful.
The meaning is that gold is surpassed by the beauty of his complexion, and the moon by the loveliness of his face.
In this case as well, according to the *vṛtta* school, the deity of the meter is Śakkarībhūṣaṇa.
Some call this *siṃhalalita*;
likewise, Jayadeva states: "And *siṃhalalita* is said to consist of the syllables *bha*, *ja*, *sa*, *na*, and *ga*."
"Quelled," and so forth.
O you who enjoy the nectar of meditative absorption— a pure intellect flowing forth, free from obscuration and with all conceptual proliferation stilled—
your unconquered ascetic discipline, which has destroyed the prowess of your enemies, subdues the three worlds.
The self-restraint of your Sage, O Muni, is that which is appropriate for ascetics;
it subdues and disciplines the three worlds, which could not be conquered by other external sages.
Of what nature is it?
By whom the prowess of the enemies—the obstructors—was destroyed.
Of what kind was the Blessed One?
He by whom the entire manifold world (*prapañca*)—the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the grasped and the grasper, and so forth—has been pacified, that is, brought to a state of cessation.
And that which is "unobstructed" is the absence of veils;
for one who partakes of that nectar, which consists precisely of those two—pure wisdom and concentration—which spread forth respectively by means of those two.
In the case of the *vṛtta* (metrical) variety, it is the *aparājitā*, adorned with *śakvarī*;
and that has the "sages" (*muni*) as its pause (*yati*).
The sages are seven.
"Terrifying," and so forth.
Out of compassion for those whose bodies are terrifying, in order to pacify their cruel conduct,
your row of mace-like arms— extremely formidable— shines forth in some places as blossoms of various weapons.
In some particular state, such as that of Vajrabhairava and others, there shines forth a most formidable array—a multitude—of your staff-like arms.
Of what nature is it?
It is such that it "wields various weapons," formed with the suffix *ṇvul*.
For what purpose?
For the sake of pacifying through compassion that terrifying and fearsome form and that pitiless conduct which they possess.
In the *vṛtta* variety, it is *śakvarībhūṣaṇā* and *praharaṇakalikā*; for others, it is *praharaṇakalitā*,
with a pause (*yati*) at the seventh syllable.
And thus Śānti says: "praharaṇakalitā nanavinanavitaiḥ. In Jayadeva's [treatment], however, there is no fixed pause (yati), according to the sūtra: "praharaṇakalitā ca nanabhanalagaiḥ."
"Superiority," and so forth.

O Giver of Boons, for those who desire that supreme state—which is the enjoyment of the highest good, undistracted withdrawal from sense objects, the destruction of Māra, the attainment of welfare for the three worlds, and which is difficult to reach and cannot be taken away—there is no other direction than devotion to You; it is not obstructed by any other quarter.
The word "śreyaḥ" (the auspicious) refers to merit (*puṇya*), and the enjoyment of universal monarchs and the like arises from that; the word "tat" (that) is connected to each [term].
Therefore, it refers to those subjects who desire that auspicious enjoyment.
O Giver of Boons, there is no other direction free from obstruction than devotion to you; there is no other path free from the perils of adversaries.
Having spoken of worldly prosperity, he now speaks of the supramundane.
And not only for those of the Śrāvaka lineage who desire that renunciation from objects— the five strands of sensual pleasure such as form and so forth—
but also for the destruction of Māra,
as well as for Bodhisattvas, the attainment and acquisition of the welfare of the three worlds.
And that state is difficult to attain and cannot be taken away from those who desire it;
"there is no other direction than devotion to you"—this is to be applied everywhere.
In the case of the *vṛtta* (metre), there are five objects (*viṣaya*).
Among those, for poets desiring restraint, there is the ornament called Śakvarībhūṣaṇā, which is unimpeded.
"Of you," and so forth.
If someone with senses restrained and intellect steady through devotion meditates upon even a fraction of you at any time,
this earth— adorned by the girdle of the ocean— will surely of her own accord choose that person before long.

If someone, with senses restrained, in some place such as a mountain cave or similar location, meditates upon even a fraction of your state— such as the stage of immovability— while possessing a mind that is attentive, steady, and motionless due to the absence of distraction;
[the word] "anything" (*kimapi*) is an adverbial modifier.
Then, before long, the Earth herself will certainly and decisively choose this person without being asked; that is to say, she will present herself for him as a *svayaṃvara* (self-choice marriage).
Of what nature is she? She has the ocean as her girdle, like the *śakkarī* meter, which is her ornament.
"Śakvarī is the metre of the girdle," says Rabhasa.
The earth is adorned with the *śakvarī* meter in its circular aspect;
it is characterized by the five senses being restrained and having attained the cessation of worldly activity through disciplined study.
"Sweat," and so forth.

Even the celestial women of the gods, as they attempt to remove their garments that are bursting open due to the swelling of thrills caused by the flow of perspiration, wear your form—which is charming with its luster, composed of the *atiśakvarī* meter, and characterized by the manifestation of Love through great trembling—as if it were a lover. (81)
In your assembly, in your court,
the celestial women manifest the sport of the bodiless god [Kāma].
Of what kind?
Where the bodice is bursting open; by what means?
By those throbbings and eruptions of lovely horripilation that manifest through its own fullness.
Likewise, it has surpassed the essence, strength, and tremor of the thighs characteristic of the *śakkarī* meter;
furthermore, what is it like?
It is as if it were charming because of their very luster, even though it was wiped away by you.
The word "iva" (as if) implies that what is utterly destroyed cannot truly be beautiful;
or rather, it means "as if beautiful" due to your own loveliness,
for it is only when there is mutual passion that the activity of Love becomes charming.
And because the Blessed One is free from passion, it is only the celestial nymphs who, upon beholding the Blessed One’s splendor, bear that [splendor] as if it were amorous.
In the section on meters (*vṛttapakṣa*), that composition which is in the *atiśakkarī* meter consisting of fifty syllables is called *anaṅgavijṛmbhita*, the essence of excellence.
This heading, "the essence of the *atiśakkarī* composition," applies up until [the end of] the section on the collection of jewel-like qualities (*guṇamaṇinikara*).
"Anupama," and so forth.

Victorious is this body, garlanded with the splendor of expansive beauty—the supreme abode of victory over the unbroken hosts of Indras—whose incomparable and charming grace captivates the heart even amidst all other noble forms. (82)

The devotion (*bhakti*), acting as the agent, which is charming through its incomparable grace (*bhaṅgi*) in the limbs and members of that Blessed One’s body, takes away the delight from all those other forms of the Blessed One himself— whether they be the various forms such as Yama and others, or specific forms such as Hari and Hara— which are noble and great.
Because of this very [attainment], there is delight right here;
thus, this body, beginning with the "royal play" (mahārājalīlā), is victorious.
Of what nature is it?

She who possesses a garland whose splendor (*rūc*) extends for a *vyāma*— that is, the supreme abode or station of victory belonging to the beauty of the unbroken rainbow (*ākhaṇḍaleṣvāsa*, Indra’s bow)—
is thus described;
for the Blessed One possesses a natural *vyāma*-wide radiance extending in all directions.
And that radiance is five-colored.
In the case of the *vṛtta* meter, because it is connected here by changing the gender to "the essence of the *atiśakvarī* composition" (*atiśakkarībandhasāra*),
this *mālinī*, which has the *atiśakvarī* composition as its essence, is victorious—
[beginning with] the words "unimpaired" (*avikala*) and so forth.

In your assemblies, O Jina who has joyfully accepted the burden [of teaching], Sarasvatī—the mistress of her own majesty—joyfully proclaims the *madraka* dance, accompanied by the sweet, melodious, and harmonious tinkling of cymbals and the beautiful fifth note (*pañcama*) produced by lutes entwined in rhythmic interplay. (83)
He who has been authorized and approved by the Jina as the bearer of the burden of others' welfare is thus awakened;
he desires your own majesty, your innate greatness. Therefore, that speech of his is led to your assemblies, where it proclaims the Madraka—a particular kind of passionate melody.
Of what nature was it?
It was *kākalī*, which possesses a *kala*—a sound that is indistinct yet sweet—characterized by an *avikala* (unimpaired) and *samasta* (complete) tempo (*tāla*).
The distinction [between *kala* and *kākalī*] arises from the relationship of general property and particular instance.
That very sound, mixed with that [other] through their union, is the *vallakī*—the lute; she by whom the beautiful fifth note (*pañcama*) is produced therefrom.
In the *vṛttapakṣa*, the *kāminī* is characterized by the *atiśakvarī* meter;
in the *ratnākara*, it is the *samudraka*.
"Victorious," and so forth.

Victorious is your arm, O Lord, adorned with armlets resembling a network of chains used to immobilize the world-conquering elephant; it is a great bolt for the door of the path to misfortune, a crusher of the pride of the God of Love, and the beloved of the Sugata. 84.
O Lord, in this particular state of yours, your arm alone—acting as a great bolt upon the path to miserable rebirth—is victorious, for it serves as a tree providing rest for the virtuous.
Regarding the word *argala*, the *Rabhasa* lexicon states: "The term *argala* has three genders.
Of what nature is it?
The elephant that conquers the world is rendered motionless by him;
he is adorned with armlets and bracelets that resemble such a network of chains.
Likewise, he is the crusher of that very Manmatha who possesses such preeminent intoxication;
for this reason, he is dear to the Sugatas.

In the case of the *vṛtta* (metre), here too, through the transformation of case endings (*vibhaktivipariṇāma*) and their connection, there is that which is called "dear to the Sugata" (*sugatapriya*), whose essence is the *atiśakkarī* bandha.
In the *Padyālaṃkāra*, it is stated: "Now, the *vṛṣabha* is called *sugatapriya*.
Regarding the commentary on the sūtra, it should be considered whether [the author] refers to "the excellent wise ones" (*varabudhaiḥ*) or to "the venerable Ratnākara" (*ratnākarapādaiḥ*).
Because this meter is not mentioned in the treatises on prosody (*chandaḥ-śāstra*),
it is now called *vāleyī* due to its similarity to the *gaditā* meter.
"Your," and so forth.
O Lord, whose greatness of virtues is honored at the summit of existence, who are pure and free from all stains,
the digit of the moon in autumn truly emulates your splendor, which has been accumulated through your supreme and victorious conquests.
O Lord!
The splendor of that fame which has been accumulated through the victory of you, the best of gods, among the excellent ones— indeed,
the word *hi* is used here for emphasis.
In autumn, it resembles a digit of the moon.
Of what nature is it?
It is that from which your own greatness of qualities (guṇamahimā), honored upon the head of Bhava—that is, on the summit of worldly existence (saṃsāra)—originates.
Likewise, by virtue of being free from all impurities, she is pure.
Even the digit of the moon, residing upon the head of Bhava, the Great Lord, is a source of great honor;
for it is pure, being free from all stains and blemishes due to its nature as a mere digit (*kalā*).
Therefore, it follows that [the self] is imitated by her.
In the *vṛtta* (metrical) category, it is the *atiśakkarī* meter, whose essence is its structural bond, known as *śaśikalā*.
"Sharp," and so forth.

This garland, fashioned by the young consort of the Lord of the Immortals, fragrant with intense perfume and swarming with young bees, providing a bliss befitting the Sugata, and possessing a delightful luster, shines upon your head. (86)
This garland fashioned by the young women of the Lord of the Immortals shines upon your head;
it possesses a *śleṣa*, which is a fusion (*laya*) of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and nectar (*makaranda*).
Of what nature is it?
She who increases the appropriate, heightened bliss of the young bee when it encounters her intense fragrance— she,
being present there through that very union with exquisite fragrance,
is like that garland which overcomes the delusion of the young bee.
In its metrical form, this garland shines forth, its essence being the *atiśakvarī* meter;
and it possesses the six rasas, as well as *laya* and *bhaṅga*.
"No," and so forth.
Since you do not resort to the station of an ascetic and since you spread throughout the world those of supreme wisdom who perform deeds for the benefit of others,
the sky— its own collection of jewels eclipsed— produces the appearance of a mass of snow in your presence.

Since you do not tread upon the path of those ascetics of peaceful form who have transcended compassion and fortitude— meaning that, O gentle-natured one, having abandoned your mild disposition, you seem to subdue them with a wrathful form—
and since you spread abroad in this world the welfare of others, being skillful and wise; such is the sense.
Therefore, the mass of your virtues, possessing the brilliance of a heap of snow, produces the sky; that is to say,
it creates a space whose own jewel— the sun— is eclipsed because it has been darkened by the multitude of the gems of your virtues.
In the case of the *vṛtta* meter, it is the essence of the *atiśakkarī* composition, a collection of strings of jewels.
Iron is well known as being of eight kinds;
therein, *pada* refers to the pause (*yati*).
"Having passed beyond," and so forth.

O You whose multitude of virtues is beyond counting, how could even the most eloquent speech ever reach the limit of Your qualities? For the collection of jewels of Your virtues is as immeasurable as the ocean, even by ascetics of perfect discipline who have measured the depths of the seas.
For whom there is a story that produces excessive delight;
"uninterrupted" because of the absence of any break; "ever-new" meaning different from one another.
"Whose praise is new," and likewise "whose qualities are uncounted"—these three are all vocative terms.
To the question "By whom are they uncounted? he replies:
By supreme ascetics.
Of what kind?
By those whose discipline (*yati*)—that is, self-restraint (*saṃyama*)—is excellent.
How could the collection of jewels existing within the oceans ever equal the measure of your multitude of virtues?
The meaning is that, because your virtues are immeasurable, it can never attain such equality.

In the *vṛttapakṣa* (metrical interpretation), it should be understood that the "mass of jewel-like qualities" (*guṇamaṇinikara*) is characterized by a pause at every group of four syllables, due to the use of the plural form "in the oceans" (*udadhiṣu*) or through the grammatical principle of *ekaśeṣa*.
Thus, the *Padyālaṃkāra* states: "In each and every ocean, the mass of jewel-like qualities."
Its distinction from the previous [meter] lies merely in its caesura;
however, by virtue of the beauty of its recitation, it possesses the quality of *jitvara*.
Thus ends the section on the essence of the *atiśakkarī* meter. || 15 ||
"Victorious," and so forth.

Victorious is this body of yours, O you of exceeding compassion, which is like the earth—appropriately enjoyed by the entire world—and which possesses unshakable fortitude here, having overcome the manifold doubts of all people through methods that surpass even the intellect of children. 89.
His compassion is exceedingly vast;
here, this body of his triumphs.
Alas, how much more so is the entire earth fit for the enjoyment of its enjoyments?

Thus, she possesses an unshakable resolve and fortitude. By whom is she unshakable? She is not shaken by the various playful maneuvers of the diverse misconceptions and contradictions of all people who are possessed of a small, immature intellect.
Regarding the section on *vṛtta* (syllabic meters), he will state that there are eight [varieties]. These eight [varieties] in a meter of sixteen syllables are named *acaladhṛti*.
For others, these serve as examples within the *mātrāsamaka* class of meters.
"Dependent upon," and so forth.

O you whose auspicious manifestation is exceedingly weighty, even one of dull intellect perceives your collection of virtues as having a balanced burden—like a blue lotus placed in the palm of the hand—just as one of tender mind perceives the blue-lotus-like lineage of the Jinas. || 90 ||
An address to him whose compassion is exceedingly heavy toward those of dull intellect;
he who possesses an auspicious collection [of qualities] that is itself auspicious and the cause of auspiciousness;
likewise, he by whom the blue water-lily (kuvalaya) has been placed within the palm of his hand.
This too is a double entendre.

Here in this world, even a person of dull intellect perceives the *jinakuvalaya*—the lotus-like Jina who possesses the circle of the stages beginning with *muditā* (joy)—as a *kuvalaya* (water-lily) that is not difficult to carry because its weight is not uneven.
For you are one who holds the *kuvalaya* (earth-globe) in the palm of your hand; thus, there is a play on words (*śabdacchala*).
In the case of the *vṛtta* (metrical) variety, there are eight [syllables] and it is an unprecedented *kuvalaya*.
And because of the identity of *ḍa* and *la*, it is so called because it has a pause (*yati*) directed toward the ocean (*jaladhi*).
"Space," and so forth.

O Lord, you shall display here in the interior of this world-forest the noble gait of a bull-elephant—triumphant over the clouds, shattering the pride of the multitude of intoxicated elephants that are the lofty disputants, whose rutting spray is the pervasive fragrance of your fame scattered across the sky. 91.
O Lord! He is the bull, the most excellent; and he is that very elephant.
The word *ṛṣabha* is a synonym for "auspicious" (*bhadra*) and "excellent" (*śreṣṭha*). Accordingly, there is the usage: "I roar the lion’s roar of the bull" (*ārṣabhaṃ siṃhanādaṃ nadāmi*).
It is not a comparison with the earth, as it would otherwise have been expressed as *gajarṣabha*.
You bear here within the belly of the universe his noble manifestation; what kind of manifestation?

One from which the multitude of haughty, trumpeting, and rutting elephants of opposing disputants is shattered by the perception—and thus the smelling—of the fragrance of his own fame, which is scattered throughout the sky.
For indeed, upon smelling the scent of the rut-fluid of the scent-elephant (*gandhagaja*), other elephants are seen to become intoxicated;
furthermore, what is it like?
It is a roar, a thundering.
In that context, *yati* means effort;
it is he by whom the rain-cloud was conquered through such [effort].
In the case of the *vṛtta* (metrical) variety, there are eight [syllables] in the *ṛṣabhagajavilasita*;
it is that in which the pauses (*yati*) occur at the seventh and fourth syllables.
"Ka" and so forth.
O you who have shattered your vow with the intent of bestowing the welfare of the world, while you stand clad in armor, where is there even a spark of remorse?
For the hand of the women of Māra’s retinue remains merely languid in fashioning decorative leaf-designs upon their lovely cheeks.

In you—who have donned the armor of boundless vigor with the resolve to establish the welfare of the world—there is not even a particle or a trace of distress regarding any matter for the sake of others.
This is because such [suffering] is beneficial to me;
it is for this very reason that you are addressed as "one whose promise is unimpaired."
In this case of negation,
there is simply the fact that the proposition remains uncontradicted.
Why?
For this reason, on the lovely surface of the cheeks of Māra’s wives, the hand remains motionless, as the decorative patterns of fresh leaf-designs persist there because Māra has been conquered.
In the circular variety, there is an unprecedented arrangement of eight petal-breaks.
"Without peer," and so forth.
O Jina, having beheld your eight incomparably beautiful forms, the world-protectors, whose sorrows have been dispelled, are exceedingly moved;
for this youthful grace of yours, charming with its five-fold robes, is adorned by a row of toenails that shine like pure white lotuses.
O you of incomparable and beautiful form,
O dispeller of sorrow!
This maiden gladdens and delights the eight playful world-protectors upon seeing your assembly of Sugatas, who have seen the lineage of the Jinas.
"Exceedingly" means to an extreme degree.
Even for one who has seen the Son of the Jinas, this youthful playfulness is exceedingly beautiful; thus, it is a cause for extreme pride.
Of what sort is she?
She is beautiful by virtue of having fashioned for herself the five garments (pañcacīra).
Furthermore, of what nature is she? She is one whose "upadhi"—meaning gold—is here excellent (san) and beautiful (śobhana).
And that [is] the row of claws of this Puṇḍarīka tiger; thus, she is "resplendent" (rājita) by means of those two.
In the case of the meter, there are eight "graceful movements of a youth" (kumāralīlā);
beyond eight, no more are prescribed.
"Of the qualities," and so forth.

"May I possess an abundance of virtues; may this be so for the worlds as it is for me"—such was Your own spontaneous desire that attained its fulfillment, so that within You alone there arose this manifestation (*bhūti*), which brings about the discernment of the supreme essence and is the mountain-peak of all branches of happiness.
In this world,
how may that very abundance— the over-extension— of my virtues become a blessing for the worlds?

Your inclination (*cchanda*), which was a longing, gradually and naturally reached its full development and maturation; thus, in this world, the perfection (*pāramitā*) became the branch of all happiness, and the splendor of virtues, reaching the very pinnacle of that branch, arose in you alone, O Blessed One. This is because, through being intent upon the welfare of others, it brings about the excellence of one's own self-interest, [arising] from both the vow (*praṇidhi*) and the setting forth (*prasthāna*).
Of what nature is she?
She is the bringer forth of the supreme variety of rasa, that is, the specific aesthetic flavor such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra) and others.
In the section on *vṛtta* meters, the *aty-aṣṭi* meter consists of seventeen syllables; it underwent a transformation such that the *śikhariṇī* arose.

That [meter] consists of six *rasas*, its varieties are its structural divisions (*bhaṅga*), and it is the means for their composition. It should be understood that the discussion concerning the *aty-aṣṭi* meter’s transformation continues up to the *mandākrāntā*.
"Victorious," and so forth.

Victorious is the Lord of the Three Worlds, the Upholder of the Earth, whose broad chest is like the stone floor of the celestial mansions of the immortals; whose foot-knuckles possess a luster resembling a forest of lotuses on the earth; who is adorned with a manifest splendor exceeding a hundred suns; and who crushes the pride of Death.
The Buddhas are the lords of the three worlds; their "grounds" (pṛthivīs) are the stages beginning with Muditā. He who stands upon them is thus [described]. He is victorious.
Of what nature is he?
Meru is the abode of the immortals;
his chest is as vast as the boulders found thereon.
By this, his golden luster is also indicated.
Thus, his foot-lustre is like a forest of land-lotuses (*sthalīkamala*);
for lotuses arise from a root (*kanda*), and his lustre likewise emerges from the root of his feet. Because of its redness and its expansiveness, it is compared to a forest of lotuses.
"A hundred light-makers" refers to many suns.
He is adorned with a splendor exceeding that [of the sun],
because his radiance surpasses a thousand suns.
He is said to have conquered the Māra of Death by virtue of crushing the pride of Kṛtānta (the Ender).
In the case of the *vṛtta* (metre) category, the *Atyaṣṭi* metre underwent a transformation (*pariṇati*) such that the *Pṛthvī* variety of *vṛtta* emerged.
That *vṛtta* variety is "Madāmadanāṣṭamardana": *mada* (intoxication), *madana* (love), and those eight [passions]; it is that which possesses the crushing (*mardana*) and cutting (*cheda*) of them.
If, however, this were an epithet of *Pṛthvī*, it would have to be *Māmardana*.
"Vimoha," and so forth.

O Prince, sun of the lineage of the Jinas, if you have not for long cherished the joy of taking refuge at your lotus feet—the festival that dispels the dense veil of darkness through the power of delusion—then, while we remain in the perils of existence that exceed even the depths of the subterranean caves, we have been conquered by the Māras. 96.
O Prince, sun of the lineage of the Jinas and illuminator of the lineage of the Buddhas!
By living beings enveloped by the dense mass of the thick darkness of delusion, [you are seen].

If the bliss characterized by the festival of taking refuge at your lotus feet has not been perceived, then that very place is the subterranean realm of Pātāla; it is a cave because of its lack of light.
Thus, one remains in vain—that is, fruitlessly—amidst the perils of worldly existence which surpass even that.
And at that time, after a long interval, that which was conquered by the Māras is won back.
In the *vṛtta* version, the *aty-aṣṭi* meter undergoes a transformation such that it becomes "ramā," from which the earth (*pṛthivī*) is produced;
the distinction lies in the fact that the former "earth" (*pṛthvī*) is devoid of a pause (*yati*), whereas this [latter] "earth" (*pṛthivī*) possesses one.
O Lord, this fickle life-span, which has been brought about by hundreds of aeons as if to yield great fruit, is now offered by those devoted to bowing before you;
O descendant of the lineage of the Compassionate One who took refuge in the feet of his Guru, it is like a lotus fallen upon a leaf, cast down by the grace of its ornament-like beauty. 97.
This extremely fickle life has been made over by those intent on bowing before you;
what is it like?
It is like that great fruit which was produced and accomplished over a hundred kalpas.

Just as water falling upon the leaf of a lotus flower, though flickering, attains a state of beauty worthy of an ornament—this being said because of the excellence of its support—it has been stated: "That [water] resting on a lotus petal bears the splendor of a pearl.
Life, too, is just like that.

"Great compassion" (*gurukaruṇā*) refers to that direction or path wherein it exists. Those ascetics and sages who have taken refuge in such a direction of great compassion constitute the lineage of those who have taken refuge in the direction of great compassion.
By this, the vocative address "O you who belong to the lineage of ascetics who have taken refuge in the direction of great compassion" is established.

In the case of the *vṛtta* (metrical) variety, it is called *aty-aṣṭi*, which is a meter (*chandas*), and it undergoes a transformation such that [the phrase] "fallen like a bamboo leaf" (*vaṃśapatrapatitam*) arises; this is due to the connection through a change of gender (*liṅgavipariṇāma*).
And because its pause (*yati*) occurs in the ten directions, it is called *digyati*.
"Your," and so forth.
O Giver of Boons, it is only the gracious-faced Lord who brings forth the abundance of Your speech, purified by its affection for the expansion of Your virtues;
and Brahmā likewise [brings forth] the Sāmaveda, the abode of sweetness, accompanied by the Yajurveda, which is the very source of pride for the nectar of the ears. 98.
O Varada!

Only that one whose eloquence is purified by affectionate familiarity with Your virtues can bring about such a face; no other can. For this very reason, You are "Sumukha" (the One with the Auspicious Face).
To the objection that his pleasant countenance arises simply from his familiarity with the three Vedas, he replies:
because of the sweetness of his singing, which is full of honey; and because it is also the abode, the very place, of the Sāman, a specific portion of the Veda.
And because this word "also" (api) is connected with each [term] individually,
it follows that it is also "concomitant" (anugata).
By what?
By means of the *yajuṣ*— of what nature? Accompanied by joy (*sajuṣ*), that is, delightful.
Likewise, "abhimāna" (pride) is the conceiving [of something] as having the form of the nectar of hearing; its "bhavana" (becoming) is the state of that.
In some places, there is the reading "śravaṇasudhābhidhāna" (the designation 'nectar of hearing').
Even in that case, the "bhavana" (becoming) of the designation "śravaṇasudhā" is its locus by way of being the thing designated.
A cluster (*kuṭa*) of such verses;
the suffix *ka* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*).
According to Amara, "The words *kuṭa* and *nipa* denote that which is not a tree (*astrī*)."
The meaning is that it serves as a vessel, like a jar.
Even such a face brings about a state of true beauty only when its abundance of speech becomes purified by a longing for the expansion of your virtues.
In the case of the *vṛtta* meter, when the *atyashṭi* prosodic form undergoes a transformation, the *narkuṭaka* arises.
"O you who [reside] in the three worlds," and so forth.

O Lord, your activity—honored as a blossoming mango tree in the honey of the Jina’s resolve that bestows joy upon the three worlds—is filled with the nectar of peace flowing from the clusters of your teachings; it is frequented by the bees that are ascetics and possesses the sweet warbling of the cuckoo that is your eloquent speech.
He is the Lord.
That resolve of the Jina which bestows joy upon the three worlds—the very effort to uplift the world during his state as a Bodhisattva—is itself the sweet spring (*madhu-vasanta*).
Regarding that [resolve], "sahakāra" means the act of assisting (*sahakaraṇa*).
That which is manifest is its very nature, its reality; that is its state as an auxiliary.
Honored by that [nature], your desired activity, O bee, strives to act like a nourisher;
likewise, only a person who acts is truly a cuckoo, warbling sweetly.
The suffix *kan* is used in its own sense (*svārthika*). He did not even maintain that [view]. In both cases, the singular number is used to denote a class (*jātāv ekavacanam*).
Bearing a body [of realization] through that joy which arises from drinking that nectar of peace— which has flowed and streamed forth from the *Pravacanamañjarī*—

the awakening of Noble Mañjughoṣa is bound to his will; and his activity, which serves as a cooperative cause for the liberation of the world during the causal stage, gradually increases until it encompasses the activities of all Buddhas.

Having fully awakened to them, he sustains the ascetic disciples and the accomplished Bodhisattvas through the joy of tasting the nectar of Nirvana that flows as a natural outflow from the teaching of those Dharmas.

Likewise, even though spring brings delight to the three worlds, it sustains the bees—who are naturally inclined toward the humming sounds of their activity—only through the bliss of drinking the nectar emerging from the fresh blossoms of the mango trees; for tranquility (śama) has no other essence than the cessation of affliction.
In the case of the *vṛtta* (metrical) variety, when the *chandas* is *atyaṣṭi*, it attains the form of *pariṇati*; thus the *kokilaka* arises.
In that [meter], there are six pauses (*yati*), and a *pada* is so called because it possesses such a pause.
"In some cases," and so forth.

O Lord of the Sugata, mountain that crushes the rutting elephants of the many disputants, O Sovereign of the forest of the three worlds, deep within the cavernous abode of your heart—there the fierce great army of Māra flees in haste like a doe, held back by the ocean of your delight in playful sport. (100)
The lord of the forest (*vanādhīśaḥ*) is the master of the woods.
Although the term is common to many, it specifically denotes the lion here because he crushes rutting elephants, dwells in the deep mountain caves like a serpent, and puts deer to flight.
The Blessed One (*bhagavān*) is likewise a "lord of the forest," for he is the sovereign of the three worlds as if he were the master of the woods.
The mind of the Sugatas is his own internal consciousness;
that very [mind] is his home, a deep cave within the mountain of the earth.
And he is the one who utterly destroys the intoxicated elephants of those who speak excessively.
This triad is a vocative address.
In some particular state of yours, out of fear of Māra, his fierce and great army flees and runs away swiftly like a doe.
Of what nature is it?
The "ocean" is the very essence of the rasa of play because of its vastness; the meaning is that [the world] is bound therein and dependent upon it.
In the case of the *vṛtta* (metrical) category, the *atyaṣṭi* meter underwent a transformation such that the *hariṇī* arose;
it is regulated by six aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*) and four oceans [of syllables], being joined with pauses (*yatis*).
"Of those who are difficult to tame," and so forth.

O Lord of renowned valor, for the sake of subduing those who are difficult to tame, you sometimes assume a form out of the force of your compassion, the tip of whose foot brings about the dissolution of this triple world; through its piercing cry of lamentation, the Mandākrāntā meter—whose sole function is its rhythmic flow—is rendered unstable and quickly loses its composure.
O Lord of renowned valor!

For the sake of subduing those who are difficult to tame, you assume a physical form somewhere through the surge and intensity of your compassion— a form by the tip of whose foot this triple world, though only slightly stepped upon, undergoes dissolution, that is to say, it sinks down into a state of profound absorption.
It should be understood that, being thus, one does not quickly attain health.
Of what nature is she?
She "shatters" (bhinatti) the "taste for hearing" (śruti-rasa), that is, the desire for listening; hence the suffix *kvip*.

And that is the sound of wailing (*ākrandana*); it is that which has a single mode of operation (*vṛtti*) therein. In the case of the *vṛtta* [meter], the *aty-aṣṭi* meter underwent a transformation such that the *mandākrāntā* arose.
The Śruti consists of the four Vedas and the Rasas are six; that which has such a division is described as "tathā" (of such a kind). Beyond this, the number eight is not authorized.
"Beauty," and so forth:
The perfection of beauty upon his head, produced by a single preceptor, is like that which arises from a wish-fulfilling tree bearing an auspicious jar resembling its own virtuous fruit.
And this vine-like arm of the Lord, shining with the sprout-like nails of his hand moving during his exposition, gleams like a flowering creeper swaying in the wind. (102)
Whatever excellence of splendor may belong to the *kalpadruma*, the wish-fulfilling tree—
of what sort is it?
It bears upon its head an auspicious jar (*bhadraghaṭa*), which resembles a virtuous fruit and consists primarily of the merit-fruit shared by all sentient beings.
That very [arm] becomes endowed with the weight of the Guru Akṣobhya, who is stationed upon the head of her husband Mañjuśrī.
This creeper-like arm of her husband—who is like a wish-fulfilling tree—shines like a flowering vine shaken by the wind.
How so?
She is swaying with her explanation, and she is radiant with the nails—those "kararuhas" (hand-born) which are connected to the hands (*kara-sambandhinah*).

For even in the case of two adjectives, a compound is formed when there is an intended relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) in relation to a common substantive (*viśeṣya*).

In the *vṛtta* section, that very same *mandākrāntā*—which possesses a specific pause (*yati*) and the like, resulting in a perfection of beauty—is produced at the beginning, by means of a single heavy syllable (*guru*) placed at the head; this is the *kusumitalatāvellitā*, which will be described under the meter (*chandas*) of eighteen syllables in the *dhṛti* class.
"Vṛtta," and so forth.
O you who are utterly dull-witted, if this poem—which has been placed in the heart of the moon-like treasury of the stainless lineage of all Buddhas—has been taken up by you;
and if it is held with the tongue out of affection for its wealth, essence, and pride; then surely your jeweled earring has been shattered to serve as an ear-ornament. 103.

Because the deeds already described and those yet to be told—which consist of the giving of joy to the entire family of Buddhas and so forth—have been placed and established in the heart of the Blessed One, who is a stainless storehouse of digits [of light], [the author says]: "O you great fool, O pearl necklace, you have lost [yourself]. This is connected with the word "iti" which will be used later.
Therefore, O great dullard, you have lost your pearl necklace.
The meaning is that even for you, who are already supremely cooling because you are the cause of ultimate liberation (*paramanirvṛti*), this necklace is indeed not to be discarded (*ahārya*).
If it has been made affectionate by the tongue, what is the use of the pride of its excellence as *ghanasāra*—that is, camphor? What is the use of the intoxication of being the essence of camphor?
Nothing at all;
because of its very deliciousness,
it is an ear-ornament.
If it was made into an ear-ornament,
then because of the connection with the word "even here" (atrāpi),
it is certainly determined that the jeweled earring was broken and conquered.
Because this very [work] serves as an ornament for the ear.
In the case of the *vṛtta* (round) wing, when held steady, it is indeed called *karṇapūra*, with the target clearly visible.
"Accumulated," and so forth:

Your own incomparable majesty, which seems insatiable through services that grant the comfort of Śacī’s palm and consist of an accumulated store of merit, manifests itself upon the jeweled footstool as a clearly visible tamāla-leaf and *mallikā* flower when you bow before the Hundred-Holder (Indra). 104.
He has accumulated a store of merit; his majesty is unequaled;
for you there is a footstool slab made of jewels.
Because it was fashioned by the palm of Śacī’s hand, it is as if never satiated— even by the pleasant services and honors offered by that very palm; thus,
now that the hundred-sacrificing Indra (Śatadhṛti) bows down from his forehead,
he has acquired and worn as a tilaka-leaf upon his brow a leaf from the *tamāla* tree.
It makes its own self manifest as such;
that is to say, it reveals it as satisfied.

Even for one who eats—that is, even for one gratified by causes of pleasure such as the palms of a beautiful woman’s hands or by side-dishes and the like—it is only the tilaka on the forehead that indicates satisfaction.

Likewise, even for the Blessed One, who has accumulated a mass of merit and possesses incomparable majesty, such a footstool made of jewels does not manifest its satisfaction through the palms of the hand of the woman named Śacī, though she stands there with ease; rather, it manifests its fulfillment only when the dark tamāla-leaf mark is transferred from the forehead—the supreme limb—of the sacrificer of a hundred sacrifices as he bows down.
In the case of the *vṛtta* (metre), it clarifies that the *tamāla* leaf is unprecedented.
Where?
It exists among the eleven *bhava*s (forms of Śiva).
The word "in the case of *dhṛti*" is excluded.
"For the sake of others," and so forth.
O Lord, I shall relate the various sentiments unfolding from the face of universal compassion of those who are steadfast in the welfare of others and possessed of supreme fortitude;
O Teacher, grant me for even a moment that purifying state of those who purify all, by which you strike down the thundering clouds of my sins and the darkness surrounding me on every side. (105)

O Lord of the Bodhisattvas who remain steadfast for the sake of others and possess supreme fortitude! Those various flavors are the diverse kinds of aesthetic delight (rasa) and yearning found within those [experiences].
Thus, compassion for the entire world is Your mouth—the gateway—[and] You are the abode of those manifold flavors that unfold [therein].
This too is an address:
"Listen," that is, hear; "I shall inform you."
He asks: "What do you request? [The disciple] says: "O Guru, among all purifying things, bestow upon me even for a moment that purifying state by which You take away the manifestations of my sins."
Of what nature are they?
They are those from which all darkness has completely vanished.
In the *vṛtta* variety, when there is an excess of *dhṛti*— that is, in a meter consisting of nineteen syllables— it is agreed upon by the wise as *meghavisphūrjitā*,
which has a pause (*yati*) at every six syllables.
May he protect, and so forth.

May Mañjuśrī protect you—he who is the moon for the increase of the ocean of the noble lineage of the Buddhas; who has surpassed all talk of the god of love in his union with the lady of Wisdom (Prajñā);
and who, in the battle against the deer-like universal afflictions, displays the prowess of a tiger, possessing a brilliance that overcomes the terrifying night of delusion like that of the sun. 106.
The lineage of the excellent Buddhas is itself an ocean due to its vastness and other qualities; may Mañjuśrī, who is like the moon that causes that ocean to swell, protect you all.
His wisdom is non-dual intellect, which is his consort; yet, even in her company, he has surpassed all talk of the god of love—this constitutes an apparent contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*).
Furthermore, of what nature was he?
He maintained the conduct of a *yati* (ascetic) belonging to the Sun.
For what purpose?

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: that very ignorance which is a terrifying and fearful delusion is the "night" (*vibhāvarī*); in its overcoming, there are likewise the afflictions of the entire universe, which are like "deer" (*kurañga*); and the Lord, assuming the play of a tiger (*śārdūla*) or a leopard (*dvīpin*) in the act of combat against them, is thus described.
In the case of the *vṛtta* (metrical) variety, by changing the gender through grammatical connection, it is the *śārdūlavikrīḍita*, possessing extreme steadfastness;
it bears twelve *yatis* (caesuras) in its radiant [feet].
"Antar-ityādi" (and so forth).

O crusher of fierce planets, seeing the state of your victory over the three worlds, the hosts of gods and sages were broken by the hairs standing on end on your body due to the sprouts of inner fear;

yet, for the sake of performing every kindness toward those with faces like the treasure of priceless smiles, you rose from the lunar orb—which was surrounded by the pure rays of your stainless arrows—out of compassion.
"Smiling" (*smita*) is the very wealth (*vasu*); that which possesses this is "smiling-wealth. This is an address to one whose face possesses priceless smiling-wealth.
To the question "From whom [did you obtain] such [a state]?", he says "O Immaculate One" (*amala*), and so forth.
He asks: "For what reason was that? [The answer is:
"In order to do what is pleasing for the entire multitude of sentient beings.

Having seen those states of yours—such as the fierce planets, the subduer of the three worlds, and the wrathful [deities]—or having seen that form which conquers the three worlds, [the enemy] was broken.
By which multitudes of divine sages and assemblies of celestial seers?
Of what kind were they?
They were those whose body hairs stood on end and bristled, appearing like sprouts from the seed of internal terror.
Of what nature are you?

You are one who, out of compassion, is intent upon the welfare of the world, and who, out of pity, has a smiling face for the sake of bringing joy to the world; yet this present state of yours seems contradictory. If you say this, it is not so, because ultimately, by demonstrating fear, it brings about the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*).
In the section on *vṛtta* (fixed meter), regarding the *suvadanā* meter consisting of twenty syllables:
there, "broken by groups of sages" means that the break (*bhaṅga*) occurs every seven syllables; this is the sense of *yati*.
The word "in [the work] composed" (*kṛtau*) indicates that the discussion of *vṛtta* continues as long as it is under consideration.
"Out of fear," and so forth.

May your lion’s sport for the sake of the world be like a companion to the gods—who, terrified by fear, have fled to great distances—when they seek refuge with their leaves spread wide; may it manifest the minds of those devoted to their Guru with intense reverence; may it possess the immeasurable speed of the sky; and may it shatter the serpent-like roar of the clouds at the end of the age on all sides, destroying Māra. 108.
May there be for the world such a playful sport of you, the Lion, by which Māra was shattered on all sides; what kind [of sport]?
One characterized by vehicles such as Airāvaṇa and others, whose wings were broken by fear, like those of separated lovers.
Since the gods, coming to take refuge in you, had their mounts terrified and cast down from afar by the fear of your lion’s sport (*siṃhavikrīḍita*),
they consequently became manifestly possessed of even greater devotion toward you due to the shattering of their egoism.
Therefore, when their minds are overflowing with devotion, it is indeed your lion’s sport itself that provides the assistance.

The intention is that because the mind becomes filled with devotion through approaching the guru while avoiding [using] vehicles and such, the teacher’s instruction—which is the manifestation of that very devotion—has that [devotion] itself as its auxiliary cause.
In the case of the *vṛtta* (metrical) category, when [the feet] are composed as *siṃhavikrīḍita*, that is where there are thirteen *māra*s (syllables) in the *khaṇḍitā*;
for it is recited thus: "Indeed, eight, eight, six, and five."
True;
however, because the arousal of the Smaras occurs starting from each step up until the thirteenth step, they are said to be thirteen.
As it is stated in the commentary on the verse "This composition, by its lordly nature, calls to mind the Smara-weapon, and thus becomes the Siṃhavikrīḍita," where it says, "The Smaras are thirteen."
And this is the distinction: it is the same *śārdūlavikrīḍita* meter, with the difference that there are two short syllables (*laghu*) in place of the first long syllable (*guru*).
"Pervaded," and so forth.

With an intellect that pervades the universe and is as utterly pure as the autumnal sky, you have developed a sublime compassion directed toward the immeasurable realm of sentient beings who are distressed by unbearable suffering;
O best among speakers, you who are forever non-abiding in both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa—such conduct belongs to no one else, not even by name, for it does not lead to the attainment of liberation.
With an intellect that has pervaded the universe and is as utterly pure as the autumnal sky, he has taken refuge in [that wisdom];

and being distressed and agitated by unbearable suffering, he is moved by the compassion that depends upon the immeasurable realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*)—that very compassion which is his essential nature.
Thus, within *saṃsṛti*, the cycle of existence...
"Those who have no eternal foundation in cessation (*nirvṛti*) or in *nirvāṇa*—they are both those [beings] and proponents (*vādinaḥ*); to them belongs this most excellent address.
Such a conduct of yours, as has been said and will be said, does not lead to the establishment—that is, the certainty—of another even by name, that is, even by name alone.
When the two halves are equal, it is called *vṛtta*;
the term "in the case of [the halves being] made" (*kṛtau*) is no longer applicable. || 20 ||
"Intense," and so forth.

With the lords of the four quarters, whose very existence depends on the momentary restraint of your side-glances— which resemble streaks of iron melted by intense heat— and with the tenfold host of beautiful women who naturally raise themselves up, who conquer the five-arrowed god of love through their vast display of graceful charms, you spread an indescribable splendor of supreme wonder.

By means of the four wrathful ones—Yama, Antaka, and the others—who are the lords of the four directions and who possess the power to create and destroy the entire universe through their side-glances, which resemble molten iron flowing from intense heat, you manifest an indescribable splendor of exceeding wonder.
By what kind of beings? [By those whose very nature is such.]

By them, the self was thus naturally uplifted and raised up by its greatness; it was the conqueror of that five-arrowed one (Kāma), whose expansion— the spreading out of the manifold variety (*prapañca*) consisting of the play of delusion or error— is vast.
It is not by these alone;

rather, it is also characterized by a group of ten beautiful women consisting of the five goddesses beginning with Locanā and the six beginning with Vakrā. This mention of the mandala deities (maṇḍaleyas) is illustrative; others should also be understood.
In the case of the *vṛtta* class, within the *prakṛti* meter consisting of twenty-one syllables, the meter named *sundarī* is *udañcitā*.
"Engraved," and so forth.

The sky is filled with the splendor of your worship, appearing as if carved from a cluster of blossoming *kunda* flowers by the three graceful curves of glances; it is repeatedly bathed by the waves of your beloved’s radiance that wash away the body-unguents with perspiration; and it is pervaded by Vidyādhara women whose ignorance has been dispelled, who wear garlands made radiant by swarms of bees humming with joy as they are drawn by your fragrance. (111)

The sky is pervaded by Vidyādharīs who, drawn by the fragrance of garlands as if by a magnet, are delighted by the subsequent attainment of their desired objects; thus, they bear for worship those garlands made radiant by swarms of bees that hum along with them.

It is understood that the sky, being thus filled by those Vidyādharīs who delight in worshipping you, shines as if it were a mass of *kunda* flowers—carved, sown, or cast upward—that have emerged from it.
By what is it pervaded such that it appears so?
The sky was pervaded by those very Vidyādharīs with their beautiful side-glances— those glances which flicker and possess lovely curves and undulations—
and it appeared as if bathed or washed by the cosmetic ointments that had slipped away due to the perspiration born of the emotion of *sattva* upon seeing the Blessed One.
In the *vṛtta* variety, the *sragdharā* is naturally upturned;
it is characterized by three parts, each marked by seven syllables, which possess beautiful breaks and pauses.
[The term] "naturally upturned" (*prakṛtyudañcitā*) is thus concluded.
"Form" (ākṛti), etc. [is the beginning of the verse].

O Lord, O Ocean of Virtues, O Teacher whose majesty is beyond the reach of words, this traveler on the path of worldly existence— whoever always sings Your name, which is filled with excellence in form, birth, conduct, power, and sequence, and which is pure fame more beautiful than the autumnal moon, sung of to the ends of the earth— surely sings this *madrakam* dance for You.
O Blessed One, O Lord, O Guru whose majesty is inaccessible to words, O Ocean of Virtues!
That traveler on the path of worldly existence who always sings this Madraka melody consisting of Your invocation and containing Your name— he [is blessed].
Form refers to physical appearance;
birth refers to one's caste, such as that of a god and so forth;
and conduct refers to virtuous behavior.
Wealth and so forth constitute *vibhava*;
and *krama* refers to valor.
One should strive to attain these such that there is the happiness arising from their excellence and abundance.
May his fame, pure because it is more beautiful than the autumnal moon, reach the ends of the quarters.
In the section on meters (*vṛttapakṣa*), this *madraka* meter is that which has its birth in the twenty-two-syllable prosodic form (*ākṛti*). It is sung with a pause (*anta*) at the ten directions;
thus, the term "born from the form" (*ākṛtijanma*) is concluded.
"Madhvāsāra," and so forth.

O Lord of Speech, O Giver of Boons, though you possess full knowledge of the power of the mind’s transformations, you alone— having accumulated the strength of total renunciation toward wealth and sensual objects— experience in heaven the exclusive playground of the splendor of enjoyment, which is the sole abode of delight for those intoxicated by the humming of swarms of bees wandering after bathing in the essence of honey, even though you know the heart of the sage.
O Lord of Speech! O Giver of Boons!

He is a wise man (*sudhī*) who has lost all exclusive delight in the realm of wealth—that accumulation wherein there is no joy—and by whom an offering (*bali*), accumulated through the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) regarding the realm of wealth, has been presented.
He experiences constant play in heaven through the splendor of his enjoyment.
Of what nature is this?
It is a play in which there is a swarm of bees, noisy with intense intoxication, that has bathed in a shower of honey—the nectar of immortality—and subsequently hovered above it.
And because it is the one unique abode of divine play for [the Lord’s] affection,
it is therefore known as that which possesses the power even to disturb the hearts of the sages.
The meaning here is that by performing worship unto You with one's entire being, one experiences the bliss of sporting in the drinking of the nectar of heaven.
In its metrical form, there are eight Vasus (eight syllables) and five sense objects (five syllables);
that which has a pause (*yati*) at those points is *Mattākrīḍa*, within the modified meter consisting of twenty-three syllables.
"Madetyādi" (beginning with "mad") and so forth.

O Treasure of Strength, the army—whose mass of rutting elephants has surpassed the pride of the great clouds with its deep trumpeting, whose multitude of advancing troops is shrouded by the radiance of the rays from all its sharpened weapons, and which is graced by excellent warriors mounted upon superior chariots—takes refuge in the man who has you as his sole resort; it is further embellished by noble horses that move with captivating gait.

O Lord, the possessor of the ten powers, such as the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), the fourfold army takes refuge in the man who has you as his sole resort. Of what kind?
Where the multitude of elephants—with temples heavy with rut and trumpeting so as to surpass the towering clouds—has darkened the sky;
and where the host of foot-soldiers is enveloped in the garment of the radiance flashing from the rays of all their sharpened weapons.
(In some versions, the reading is *prabhāsvara*, meaning "resplendent.")
In that [army], there was a multitude of foot soldiers arrayed by rays of light from the very luminous [sun];
it also contained noble warriors mounted upon excellent chariots;
and those for whom the supreme discipline was both captivating and characterized by the non-transgression of proper conduct.

Likewise, those whose appearance is preeminent— and for that very reason, because they are well-trained, under the control of their riders, and excellent— such horses, superior by virtue of their noble breed, sported [there]. In the case of the meter, there are eleven *haras*.
Among those [mātrās], when there is a pause (yati) after the [fourth] syllable, it is called *aśvalalita*; this applies in the case of a "modification" (*vikṛti*).
The term "in the case of a modification" is understood to be excluded [from the following rule]. || 23 ||
"Joy," and so forth.

O Lord, that slender woman with a moon-like face, whose ignorance is dispelled by constantly remembering You—the abode of bliss, renowned on earth as the bestower of noble boons and supreme refuge—among those risen in the final state, she shall become exceedingly charming through the pauses of the fifth musical note arising as a companion to the play of youth; and here, she shall be under Your sway along with the Fortune of Kings.
He is the Lord,
known on earth in the stages such as the Joyous (*muditā*) by accomplished Bodhisattvas;
he whose worship and propitiation yield sublime and excellent boons.

Since you possess the final word among those [words] mentioned above that are endowed with the stated qualities, therefore, for that man who—having dispelled all doubt—constantly remembers you, the abode of bliss, the slender-faced one (the Goddess) will come under his control; she who is esteemed as the very Fortune of Kingship itself.
Of what nature is she?
The very grace that belongs to youth is her minister; she is a young woman delightful through the swoon of that ascetic who possesses the rising fifth note.
In the case of the *vṛtta* (metrical) category, that same [meter] known as *tanvī* is recognized there as a *saṃskṛta* (refined) meter consisting of twenty-four syllables.
Of what nature is it?
It has the fifth—that is, the fifth position—among the seven musical notes (*svaras*).
The pause (yati) occurs within them;
by that [pause], it is beautiful. || 24 ||
"Viśva," and so forth.
O Sovereign, that lake on earth where you—the supreme abode of wealth, whose internal organ is attached solely to the welfare of all—take up residence, becomes a place of success;

its waters are made fragrant by the ichor dripping from the temples of the elephants of the quarters as they plunge therein, and it resounds with swarms of bees hovering over golden lotus groves marked by the footprints of cranes and flocks of *sārasa* birds.

"O you who endure attachment as one and without a second for the welfare of all, because you conform to that [welfare]—this is an address to Him whose instrument, namely the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is thus directed.
Likewise, 'O Sovereign' (*adhipa*):
just as there is something well-known as the source, the place of origin, of *vasus*, which are material riches."

Likewise, because it is the cause for achieving a preeminent excellence beyond even what you desire, it is like the supreme *vasu-pada* (the station of wealth). That which manifests clearly and incessantly upon one's limbs like an immeasurable shower of drops of nectar, consisting of incomparable words of ever-fresh aesthetic flavor arising from repeated contemplation—possessing peerless splendor and not easily attained even through other various methods of meritorious action—it is that which the self-exerted person experiences here as the fruit of service to You, known as the removal of the entire flood of misfortunes. It carries away all calamities and transcends even the subtlest [obstacles].
That which is called the "remover of all calamities" is the fruit of service to You; a person whose self is disciplined experiences this in this world.

That which is not easily obtained even through other virtuous practices that are difficult and arduous to accomplish;

"Ālocanā" refers to the act of perceiving; "samudayin" refers to those nine rasas, beginning with *śṛṅgāra*, which arise in relation to that perception.

Therefore, [the phrase] means spreading clearly, continuously, and immeasurably, as if drops of nectar-essence, all around the limbs;

Victory, victory to You who sport in the form of the Lord of the Dance, whose lotus feet flash with the play of exquisite compassion, and who are praised by the serpent-king emerging from the depths of Pātāla, which are pressed down by Your swift-moving feet!

Where the cloud, driven by the fierce winds of Your unyielding staff-like arms, moves like a rain-storm upon the staff of the three worlds, seems to bring an end to exhaustion out of fear of the time of universal dissolution.

Victorious, victorious—this repetition [of "victorious"] expresses either intense emotion or frequency regarding your playful manifestation in the form of the beautiful Padyanarteśvara, which radiates through the play of compassion.

For fatigue arises from dancing, and that is dispelled by a rain-cloud showering while fanned by the wind; thus it is imagined of the Blessed One as well.
Of what sort? He is one who, as if out of fear of the time of universal dissolution (*pralaya*), punishes—that is, afflicts—the three worlds.

Indeed, when the Blessed One—desiring to favor a particular class of disciples—commenced the dance overflowing with the play of compassion, a cataclysmic dissolution (*saṃvarta*) arose through the force of the winds produced by the circle of his most wondrous, formidable, and massive arms. This dissolution, accompanied by a violent onset of darkness from the sudden, fierce torrents of rain from the clouds, caused terror to spread through the minds of those present as it violently afflicted the three worlds.
Yet, in the end, it was sweet, having resulted solely in the welfare of others.

He is truly marvelous because his tireless exertion brings about the removal of sorrow for the three worlds, which have been seized and overwhelmed by the unbearable, raging fire of misery.
He is the treasury of that conduct;

he shines as the crest-jewel and ornament of the pure lineage of the Perfectly Enlightened Ones; he is one by whom the expanse of the intermediate space is strewn—that is, pervaded—by that resplendent fame.

I bow to you, the embodiment of compassion; I bow to you, the power of compassion! You possess a body that is both incomparably fierce and filled with wonder, hidden by a firm restraint of mercy, submerged in the great ocean of non-duality, and the abode of pure qualities. Your conduct is graced by the nine dramatic sentiments of noble dance. You wear the armor for conquering the world, manifesting as a network of horripilation from the embrace of the limbs of a mature and excellent Vajra-woman. All gods and demons tremble before your wide, terrifying laughter, released through the intoxication of drinking blood and marrow along with wine. I bow to you, the power of compassion; I bow to you, the power of compassion!
Of what nature was it?
It had a shimmering network of horripilation as its armor and equipment for conquering the world;
by this much, the erotic and heroic sentiments have been expressed.
That very [blood] mixed with fat and marrow, that same honey;
by the intoxication of drinking that, the entire host of gods and demons was made to tremble by his terrifying, wide-mouthed laughter.
By this, the loathsome (*bībhatsa*), the comic (*hāsya*), and the terrifying (*bhayānaka*) sentiments are expressed.

He whose body is exceedingly firm (*gāda*), deeply hidden (*vinigūḍha*), closely embraced (*śliṣṭa*), composed of compassion and wonder (*vismaya*), marvelous (*āścaryakarī*), and incomparably fierce (*apratimaraudrā*)—

by this [description], his qualities of compassion (*kārūṇya*), wonder (*vismaya*), and ferocity (*raudra*) are indicated. *Advaya* is the reality (*tattva*) devoid of duality, such as the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*).
It is submerged in a great ocean consisting of that;
likewise, it is the abode, the locus, of pure qualities such as the ten powers (*daśabala*).
By this, it is peaceful (*śānta*).
Therefore, the suffix *matup* is used because he possesses these nine noble dramatic sentiments (*nāṭyarasa*). Likewise, it refers to one whose conduct (*vṛtta*) is graceful (*lalita*).
