In the case of the *vṛtta* meter, it is named *Vegavatī*.
"All," and so forth.

The abode of all excellence, whose splendor is characterized by auspicious marks pervading every limb—even though it has passed from the memory of the world, may that body of the auspicious Virāṭ bestow welfare upon you. 133.

"Bhadreṇa virājate" means "Bhadravirāṭ": your body, though it has entered the memory—that is, become an object of recollection—of the entire world, not only exists as such, but spreads auspiciousness (*bhadram tanoti*).
What kind [of body]?
The word *hi* (for) is displaced; because [of this reason].
The abode of splendor, which is the source of all excellence;
likewise, she whose wealth of auspicious marks (*lakṣaṇa*) is clearly visible and well-defined, pervading every limb and extending over every part of her body.
In the case of the *vṛtta* (metrical) variety, it is *bhadravirāṭ*.
"Paritaḥ," and so forth.

Your form shines forth, possessed of banners, with the beautiful, radiant rays of light— consisting of the ultimate truth for the sake of others— that flash out on all sides from your thunderbolt, lotus, sword, jewel, and discus.

O you whose supreme purpose is solely for the sake of others, your fame—bearing the banners marked by the emblems of Akṣobhya, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, Ratnasaṃbhava, and Vairocana, namely the thunderbolt, lotus, sword, jewel, and wheel—shines within the maṇḍala of the fivefold *Samāja*. By what means? By those [emblems].
The passage beginning with "paritaḥ" and so forth is easy to understand.

In the *vṛtta* variety [of meters], there is the *ketumatī*. According to the verse from the *Padyālaṃkārasūtra*, "In *ketumatī*, the pause (*yati*) occurs at the last vowel among the *svaras*," here in the first quarter, the pause is desired at the last *svara* among the *rasas*.
However, other authorities do not show those pauses.
"Mind-derivatives," and so forth.
When only mental states exist as the objects of experience, where else could such a supreme fulfillment of the welfare of others be cultivated except in compassion?

Thus, this [term *karuṇā*] is designated by the same name as the feminine form of the possessive suffix *-matup* following the word for "parts" (*avayava*), under the pretext of its outward appearance. 135.
A particular state of the mind is a mental factor (*caitta*).
That itself is "that-only" (*tanmātra*). The state of being that is "reality" (*tattva*).

And where could such a supreme fulfillment of the welfare of others—engaged in every possible way—be conceived to exist within compassion, which is of the nature of a mental factor (*caitta*) residing in that [mind], given that its object is compassion?
For, being formless (*amūrta*), it lacks the capacity to accomplish such a fulfillment of the welfare of others.

Therefore, this very compassion characterized as described above is the "disguise" (*chala*), and that [form] is the form of the Blessed One. Thus, it is from that [compassion] that [the form arises].
From the word *avayava* (part), the suffix *matup* is applied after the word *avayava-dhvani* (sound of a part);
that [suffix] itself is feminine,
because it includes the state of being terminated by a feminine suffix.
That which has a designation identical to that [imitation] which consists merely of imitation—namely, that which has the form of the object to be imitated;
the meaning is that it possesses constituent parts.
In the view that [the suffix] *matup* is present, the word *yavamatī* is formed by applying the feminine suffix *ṅīp* to *yava* because it is mentioned together with *matup*.
The absence of *vatva* (the substitution of *v* for *m*) occurs because of the prohibition against words beginning with *yava*, according to the rule *mādupadhāyāś ca mator vo ’yavādibhyaḥ*.
This arrangement of the sentences by the predecessors is based on the fact that entry into the technical terminology (*saṃjñā*) cannot be accomplished through a straightforward sequence.
Therefore, even though there is a disparity in the syllable forms to be extracted here, *śleṣa* (punning) is intended.

In that regard, for *priyaṃvadā*, *avegavatī*, *bhadravirāṭ*, and *ketumatī*, each odd quarter-verse (*ayukpāda*) consists of ten syllables, while each even quarter-verse (*yukpāda*) consists of eleven syllables.
For *drutamadhyā*, *hariṇaplutā*, *aparavaktra*, and *śiśulīlā*, the odd quarter-verses consist of eleven syllables, while the even quarter-verses consist of twelve syllables.
In the Puṣpitāgrā and Ayujmatī meters, it should be understood that the odd-numbered feet consist of twelve syllables and the even-numbered feet consist of thirteen syllables.
"Udayāditya," and so forth.

Victorious is this exceedingly beautiful body of yours, O Lord beyond existence, which is capable of acting according to the inclinations of the entire world and which triumphs over the stainless moon with its mass of golden rays like those of the rising sun. 136.
O Lord who has transcended existence (*atibhava*), this body of yours, being exceedingly beautiful, triumphs in its capacity to render the entire world lovely;
for beauty itself is indeed an act of creation.
It triumphs over both the rising golden mountain encircled by the rays of the sun and the moon, by virtue of its excellence in color and its power to delight.
It is exceedingly beautiful in its metrical form.

Regarding the term *ardhārdha*: one half consists of thirty-one syllables as an uninterrupted unit; when that half is joined with another half, it is called *ardhārdha*. In that case [the verse is formed].
If, however, it were in the dual number, there would be *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one).

The meaning is that, because the division of the *caraṇas* (quarters) is not prescribed [in that way], this very beautiful [meter] should be understood according to the other view as consisting of exactly two halves.
But in this view, the first quarter has sixteen syllables and the second has fifteen; thus, this four-lined meter is exceedingly beautiful.

And likewise, the *Padyālaṃkārasūtra* states: "With unwavering fortitude, she is the lunar day (tithi) who holds no other view; she is one whose delight is in devotion to the feet of Yama, which are free from cessation."
"O you who [reside] in the three worlds," and so forth.

Victorious is your crest-lock, which is a dwelling place for the excellence of its well-constructed joints inlaid with a multitude of pure jewels serving as companions to the images of the Blessed Sugata—who possesses the great majesty of serving the feet so difficult to attain in the three worlds;

it is a treasury of the humming of swarms of bees gathering at the fragrance of the divine flowers of the gods, which resemble the lovely sound of the bracelets on the arms of the nymphs of your own grace. 137.
Victorious is your crest-lock, O cloud of realization! Of what nature is it?
The service of his feet is difficult for the three worlds to attain because it can be obtained from him alone; for this very reason, his majesty is supreme.

It is the abode of that which is characterized by excellent craftsmanship, being inlaid with a collection of such stainless jewels as serve as the ministers for the image— the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*)— of that very Sakyamuni, the Unshakable One (*Akṣobhya*). Likewise,
it is a fragment of the subsiding— that is, the lack of excess— of the sound of proclaiming his own doctrine, the conduct of the Bodhisattvas.
That which imitates it is like a connoisseur or nearly a connoisseur;
and that which possesses the fragrance of the garlands and crest-ornaments of gods and celestial nymphs, wherein swarms of bees gather, and which has the humming sound of its tinkling— is a treasure.
In the *vṛttapakṣa* (metrical variety), there is a *śikhā*.

In that [variety], in each of the odd-numbered quarters (*pādas*), there are thirty light syllables (*laghu*) with a heavy syllable (*guru*) at the end; in the even-numbered quarters, there are twenty-eight light syllables with a heavy syllable at the end.
"Regarding 'the origin' and so forth..."

Victorious is Your sovereign speech, O Lord, which—teaching the performance of various worldly accumulations to those whose inclinations are directed toward the side of accumulation; yet possessing a vast delight in explaining the incomparable path to the bliss of tranquility to those whose minds relish the essence of the happiness of peace; which is fixedly straightforward for those of upright intellect as the fruit of immeasurable merit, while its words are exceedingly crooked for those of perverse intellect, like a vessel of nectar turned upside down. (138)
O Lord, O Amṛtakuṭa, refuge of the teachings!
Your speech, which serves as an eye because it illuminates the way of the Victors, is victorious.
Or, it is the address "O Jinanayana" (O Eye of the Victor).
Of what nature is she?
Her very arising is her direction, because she constitutes a portion of the goals of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*).

In that regard, she is one whose great delight and devotion lie in explaining the various means for the accomplishment of the origin [of suffering] to those disciples whose inclinations have been properly drawn near; and she is one whose abundant pleasure is in narrating the incomparable path to the bliss of tranquility to those whose minds are connoisseurs of the flavor characterized by the bliss of peace.
She is the outflowing fruit of immeasurable merit—the accumulation of virtue and wisdom.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
Toward beings of upright mind, its words are invariably upright and straightforward; but toward those of crooked mind, its words are unsurpassedly crooked.

In the case of the *vṛtta* (metre) category, the term *kuṭilapadā* is explained as being primarily a name for others' *khañja* [a type of metre], by virtue of its association with the word *kuṭilapadā*. "Its opposite" refers to this.
There is a reversal of the *śikhā* [meter].
Therefore, those two even feet (*yukpāda*) that occur there become the even feet here, and those two odd feet (*ayukpāda*) become the even feet here.
"Ākhyānikā," and so forth.
He who praises you, thinking, "This narrative is of your virtues," surely believes that the ocean was drunk by me through the consumption of a mere mouthful of water. 139.
Praising you by expressing your qualities through the attributes of all beings, he who considers this narrative (*ākhyānikā*)—the complete narration of your virtues—to be great;
"surely" and so forth is easily understood.
In the case of the *vṛtta* meter, it is the *ākhyānikā*.
If it is not narrative (ākhyānikā), then what is it? To this he says: "But rather," and so forth.

Moreover, O Lord, this narrative of your pride—which was previously the opposite—is now rendered false regarding those virtues that do not even admit of being described by the enemies of Smara in their entirety. (140)
But, O Lord,

regarding those qualities which do not rely on being designated as expressible, describable, or definable by all the Buddhas— the enemies of Smara— that narrative concerning them is a distorted narrative for people possessed of false pride and vain conceit.
Because there is the conceit of having explained even when there has been no explanation.
In the section on *vṛtta*, the *ākhyānikā* is that which has its first [verse] reversed.
The two types of *ākhyānikā* are varieties of *upajāti*.
Among the fourteen types of *upajāti*, two are *ardhasama* (half-equal) and the others are *viṣama* (uneven).
Among those, the two types of *ardhasama* (half-equal) meters are called *ākhyānikā* and *viparītākhyānikā*.
These have already been demonstrated in the discussion on *upajātis* within the section on poetic figures (*padyālaṃkāra*).
Thus ends the section on half-regular meters (*ardhasamavṛtta*) within the *Vivṛti* [Commentary] on the *Duṣkaraprabhedavṛttamālā*.
Now, in accordance with the order previously stated, he praises the Blessed One in a verse of uneven meter,
beginning with "With eight," and so forth.

A quarter-verse consists of eight syllables; by increasing them by one at each step until they reach twelve, and with the gaps between the digits filled by oceans [four] and oceans [four]—O Ocean of Virtues!—this *pādacaturūrdhva* meter brings about a state of unevenness within its ten stages through its compassionate nature.
O ocean of virtues, during the ten periods (*daśāntara*) such as the period of Vajrabhairava and others,
the hollow of whose fingers was not filled— that foot of yours is "unbearable" (*asodah*), meaning it is impossible to endure; the singular number is used for the class.
The meaning is "feet. By what? By the eight inexhaustible oceans of syllables.
By what means?

By those [oceans] which, though increased by the deep immersion of his foot, still serve as the enclosures for Sumeru; thus, the eight oceans—the seven outer ones and the great inner ocean—bring about, that is, cause one to attain, a form of compassion that is otherwise inconsistent with your nature or intention.
Of what nature is it? It is that in which four feet are directed upwards.
In the class of *vṛtta* meters, there is an uneven meter named *padacaturūrdhva*.
In this meter, the first quarter consists of eight syllables;
from that point onward, the subsequent quarters are to be understood as increasing successively by four syllables each.
"Thus," and so forth.

Thus, when the meter has been declared, and the arrangement of uneven feet is established, bearing a fixed sequence of light and heavy syllables—who would not be struck with fear, were it not for the restrictive rule that follows the term *abhividhi*? (142)

Thus, when birth has been described in the manner just mentioned—being inherently discordant—who would not experience fear as they proceed? Of what kind is that [birth]? It is one characterized by the arrangement of uneven steps.
In which the placement of the feet above and below has been prescribed;
furthermore, of what nature?
Bearing a fixed sequence of light and heavy syllables.
While [the author] sometimes employs brevity and sometimes gravity according to the needs of those to be instructed (*vineya*),
here only gravity is intended.
Everyone encounters fear if you do not remain strictly within the scope of the term "inclusive" (*abhividhi*).
The prefix *ā* expresses the sense of pervasiveness (*abhividhi*).
Following that [prefix], *āpīḍaḥ* means a "garland" (*pīḍa*) worn together with that [ornament].
The meaning is: "if you are not compassionate toward [us] on all sides."

In the *vṛttapakṣa*, when the *padacaturūrdhva* class has been described and the arrangement of its uneven quarters (*viṣamacaraṇa*) has been established— following the sequence of expansion (*prastāra*) for this verse and maintaining the rule of light and heavy syllables— the term "inclusive" (*abhividhi*) is explained as having the sense of "affliction" (*pīḍa*). Here, the final two pairs [of syllables] are heavy, while the remainder are light.
In the *Padyālaṃkāra*, however, the *padacaturūrdhva* is shown separately from this [work] because it lacks the elegance of the recited reading (*pāṭhasaubhāgya*) as an unrestricted [meter].
Here, however, it is stated in accordance with the ancient tradition (*pūrvāmnāya*).
"Sucira," and so forth.

This bud-like tooth of yours, resembling the crest-jewel of the Destroyer of Tripura, shines like a sprout from a tuber long stored within a well-guarded mind— its formidable form fashioned for the subduing of wicked men.

This bud-like sprout of a tooth shines like the digit of the moon— the crest-jewel of the Great Lord Maheśvara, the destroyer of Tripura, who fashioned that formidable form capable of subduing wicked folk.
Here, the first [attribute] of the *apīḍa* (the crest-jewel) becomes the second, and the second becomes the first.
The remainder is as before.
"Spreading forth," and so on.

Your playful movement of the eyes, as it forcefully turns toward you, violently pacifies even Death himself, who holds the boundless expanse of the sky like a mass of spreading, fiercely terrible, and vast funeral fires.
It pacifies even Śamana—Yama himself—who has come forward by force through the playful movement of the slight turning or glancing toward you of that eye whose form was just described.
What is it doing?
It bears the limitless sky, which, because of its density, possesses a terrible radiance spreading from the fire of its thighs, made matted with the flames of its side-glances.
In the *vṛttapakṣa* [version], it is the *lavalī*.
Here too, the first quarter-verse of the *āpīḍa* becomes the third;
the remainder is as before.
"Soft," and so forth.

Furthermore, for a person of gentle disposition, this very [speech] is surely a stream of nectar, which pacifies the entire heap of harsh and turbid poisons and repeatedly brings about a fresh, incomparable treasure of bliss. 145.

This very play of the movement of your eyes has extinguished the entire heap of the poison of bitter defilements; moreover, when directed toward a gentle person, it is surely like a stream of nectar. What is it doing?

Again and again, through the variety of her emanations, she leads those to be trained— according to their dispositions— by means of compassion toward a fresh and incomparable treasury of bliss that serves as a refuge.
In the case of the *vṛtta* meter, when the first quarter-verse of the *āpīḍa* itself constitutes the fourth [quarter], it is called *amṛtadhārā*.
The varieties of *padacaturūrdhva*.
"Taḍit," and so forth.

O Lord, this slender form of Yours, which has somehow emerged from somewhere, triumphs—though it is burdened by the weight of a mass of clouds constantly blazing with lightning and filled with the terrible roar of thick rain clouds. 146.
O Lord, this body of Yours, whose form was described immediately above, having emerged at night by some ineffable grace, triumphs over the mass of clouds;
how so?
It is radiant with lightning.
Likewise, there is a mass, a heap of water;
in that mass, the state of being water [is present];
by that, it is "bandhura," meaning bent or inclined.
And [it is] with a terrible, deep roar.

By these adjectives, which function as points of comparison (*upamāna*), the qualities of the Blessed One—the object of comparison (*upameya*)—are intimated in their respective order: the brilliance of his weapons and rays, his dark complexion and stoutness, and his fierce, dense, and loud laughter.
In the *vṛtta* (metrical) sense, this is the *udgatā* meter.

In this [meter], the first and second quarters each consist of ten syllables; the third and fourth consist of eleven and thirteen syllables respectively. The rules governing heavy and light syllables are to be determined from the corresponding *prastāra* (metrical table).
"From this," and so forth.
Therefore, as you display hundreds of such difficult-to-perform marvels,
this wondrous fragrance of your brilliant fame delights the entire world.

Therefore, it is solely by the power of your compassion that this entire world is gladdened by the potent, manifest, and wonderful fragrance, beauty, and scent of your fame as you perform hundreds of deeds more difficult than any others. For it is the convention of poets that fame is both bright and fragrant.
A profusion of white, unfading flowers fell from the sky, perfuming the quarters;
from that, his fame soared up to heaven.
And thus says Māgha.
In the *vṛtta* variety, when the third foot of the *udgatā* itself is altered as shown, it becomes the *saurabhaka*.
"Knitting the brows," and so forth.
Though Your body bears certain distortions in the form of frowns, sidelong glances, and bared teeth, it subdues the worlds; for while it is graceful, it is also formidable in such a manner.
Your body, though graceful and captivating, subdues the worlds.
One might object: "Is it not fitting that the subduing of the worlds belongs to the Terrifying [form]? To this he replies:
"But rather, it is when the teeth are joined with a frown and a sidelong glance that they become formidable."
The plural number is used due to the diversity of the relatives.
"Something" (*kimapi*) is an adverbial modifier of the action. Therefore, such a formidable form as yours is being borne.

In the case of the *vṛtta* meter, when the third foot is altered from its original form as shown, it is called *lalita* by the ancients; however, since it is of such a nature, it is more appropriate to call it *vikaṭa*.
The varieties of the *udgatā* meter.
"Prāgbhāra," and so forth.

Even upon such an extraordinary and terrifying mountain slope, which brings destruction to the world, your horse, though galloping with exceeding speed, does not equal it, moving gracefully in every direction at once.

Even that playful, slow-moving gait of yours, which was taken with ease for the destruction of the world’s enemies, though it was directed toward a place as exceedingly difficult and wondrously terrifying as the very edge of the precipitous slopes of Mount Sumeru and other mountains—where even the great velocity of the wind cannot equal it, being of no superior speed; even such a gait was taken by you. *Note: The term "prāgbhāra" refers to the sloping or precipitous side of a mountain. The verse describes how the Lord’s slow, deliberate pace toward the edge of the world (the cosmic periphery) was effortless despite the extreme difficulty and terror of the location.*
O Blessed One, why should anyone further take refuge in you, who bear the firm burden of the peerless leadership of the sages?
For that very qualification of being the Pure Virāj places its foot upon the head of another who is otherwise unequalled. 150.
Having propitiated you through the singular fulfillment of my intention, whatever stainless merit has been gained while increasing—
may all of this, which bestows great benefit upon the world, flourish through various specific modes of conduct that are dear to you.
Moreover, through this abundant accumulation of virtue, which is pure by its very nature, may the entire mass of darkness arising from the night of existence vanish for every embodied being. (152)
All poisons.

Moreover, may he here experience the bodiless dalliance through the embrace of his beloved Mature Wisdom, bearing a body composed of the mass of splendors of the Moon-Lord, which possesses unsurpassed compassion. 153.
Half-uneven [meter].

May the world, having become free from sorrow through this description of various modes of conduct—which is pure, auspicious, and bright as the rays of the moon—become the lord of the companion to the crest of great, shimmering bliss. 154.
A disorder of the feet.
The *Vṛttamālāstuti*, a hymn consisting of various difficult verses in praise of Noble Mañjughoṣa, is completed.
This is the work of the great scholar and elder Jñānaśrīmitra.
